title: Form 10-K Cover
summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s 2021 Form 10-K identifies the registrant, incorporation, tax ID, headquarters and contact details; lists its NYSE and NYSE Arca common, preferred depositary shares, exchange-traded notes and guaranteed notes, with no Section 12(g) securities; and reports filing and interactive-data compliance, large accelerated filer status, audited internal-control attestation, and non-shell status. It gives nonaffiliate common-stock market value and shares outstanding, and incorporates specified portions of its 2022 proxy statement for Part III items.

title: Form 10-K Index
summary: The text is a Form 10-K index covering Parts I–IV: business overview, segments, competition, human capital, regulation, banking assets and performance, securities, loans, deposits, and credit-loss allowances; risk factors, staff comments, properties, legal proceedings, mine safety, and stock matters; MD&A, market risk, financial statements, accounting matters, controls, other disclosures, and foreign-inspection restrictions; governance, executive compensation, ownership, related transactions, director independence, auditor fees, and exhibits and financial statement schedules.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business.
JPMorgan Chase Overview and Business Segments
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is a Delaware-incorporated, U.S.-based global financial services firm with $3.7 trillion in assets and $294.1 billion in stockholders’ equity at year-end 2021, serving consumers, businesses, and global institutions. The text describes its principal bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries, international operations, website disclosures and codes of conduct and ethics. Its activities are reported through four segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus Corporate.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase competes with a wide range of financial and nonfinancial firms offering similar or emerging products and services. Competition is based on product and service quality and variety, execution, innovation, reputation, and price, and varies by customer, industry, geography, and whether competition is global, national, or regional. New entrants include internet-only financial firms and nonfinancial companies offering payment or lending products.

nodes.title: Human Capital
key_items: Firm culture; Attracting and retaining employees; Developing employees
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its human-capital strategy for employees, excluding contractors: attracting, developing and retaining a diverse, inclusive workforce. It reports 271,025 employees across 62 countries at year-end 2021, with regional and business-line distributions, and self-reported diversity data for employees, senior leaders, the Operating Committee and Board, with definitions and coverage limitations. The text outlines core cultural values, inclusion initiatives and resource groups; recruiting, career opportunities, fellowships and skills-based hiring; onboarding, training and leadership development; and competitive, equitable compensation and extensive health, financial, family and wellness benefits, including COVID-19 protections.

nodes.title: Supervision and regulation
Financial holding company:
key_items: Consolidated supervision; Permissible business activities; Capital and liquidity requirements; Stress tests
Resolution and recovery; Orderly liquidation authority; Holding company as a source of strength; Regulation of acquisitions; Ongoing obligations
Holding company as a source of strength
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is extensively regulated in the U.S. and abroad. The Federal Reserve supervises the holding company on a consolidated basis, while subsidiaries answer to banking, securities, derivatives, and foreign regulators. Rules govern permissible activities, capital, liquidity, leverage, annual stress tests and capital plans, enhanced risk and governance standards, and recovery and resolution planning. The Firm may face orderly liquidation, must support depository subsidiaries, and is subject to acquisition limits and approval or notice requirements. It also has ongoing obligations under a 2020 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement and a related CFTC order.

nodes.title: Subsidiary banks:
key_items: FDIC deposit insurance; FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency; Prompt corrective action; OCC Heightened Standards
FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency
Dividend restrictions; Depositor preference; Consumer supervision and regulation
nodes.summary: The text outlines regulatory requirements affecting JPMorgan Chase’s banks and financial businesses: OCC authority and heightened risk-governance standards; FDIC deposit insurance and insolvency powers; prompt corrective action and possible parent-company support; affiliate-transaction, dividend, and depositor-priority rules; U.S. and U.K. consumer-protection oversight; securities and broker-dealer regulation; investment-management and fiduciary obligations; and comprehensive derivatives rules on capital, margin, clearing, trading, collateral, conduct, records, reporting, and anti-fraud, including relevant U.S., EU, and U.K. regimes.

nodes.title: Banking, Securities, and Investment Regulation
nodes.summary: The page covers affiliate transaction and borrowing restrictions, bank dividend limits, depositor claim priorities, and consumer-protection oversight in the U.S. and U.K., including regulation of JPMEL and Nutmeg. It describes U.S. and international broker-dealer supervision and rules governing securities activities, as well as global regulation of asset and wealth management, SEC-registered advisers’ fiduciary duties, state securities laws, and OCC oversight of bank fiduciary activities.

nodes.title: Derivatives regulation:
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Firm’s regulatory obligations: derivatives rules covering capital, margin, clearing, trading, reporting, dealer registration and conduct; extensive evolving data, privacy, cybersecurity and technology laws; anti-money-laundering, customer due diligence and economic sanctions requirements; anti-corruption laws; and domestic and international oversight of compensation practices. It also describes proposed U.S., U.K. and EU regulatory changes, including MiFID II transparency, market structure and trading reforms, a consolidated tape proposal, U.K. reviews, and delayed CSDR mandatory buy-in rules.

nodes.title: Regulatory Requirements and Oversight
key_items: The Bank Secrecy Act and Economic Sanctions:
nodes.summary: J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is registered with the CFTC as a futures commission merchant and belongs to the National Futures Association. The Firm faces extensive, evolving U.S. and international requirements governing data privacy, security, technology, and related practices. It must maintain risk-based anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing controls under the Bank Secrecy Act, meet reporting and customer-due-diligence obligations, and comply with U.S., EU, U.K., and other economic sanctions. Anti-corruption laws include the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and U.K. Bribery Act. U.S. and international regulators oversee compensation practices to discourage imprudent risk-taking; evolving rules and guidelines may affect compensation programs.

nodes.title: Other significant international regulatory initiatives:
nodes.summary: The text outlines U.K. and EU financial regulatory reforms: proposed MiFID II changes to transparency, market structure and an EU consolidated tape, alongside the U.K.’s Wholesale Markets Review; delayed EU CSDR mandatory buy-ins and the U.K.’s decision not to adopt the settlement discipline regime; proposed derivatives clearing and trading obligation changes reflecting the shift from IBOR to risk-free rates; implementation of Basel III standards and pending framework revisions; EU intermediate parent undertaking requirements for certain non-EU banks by December 30, 2023; and PRA/ECB supervisory expectations for banks’ climate-related financial risk strategy, governance, management, analysis, reporting and disclosure.

Covers JPMorgan Chase’s extensive U.S. and international supervision as a consolidated financial holding company and through its banking, securities, investment, and derivatives subsidiaries. Topics include capital, liquidity, stress testing, governance, resolution, acquisitions, enforcement obligations, bank safety and deposit rules, affiliate transactions, dividends, consumer protection, fiduciary duties, and derivatives regulation. It also addresses privacy, cybersecurity, AML, sanctions, anti-corruption, compensation oversight, and evolving U.K., EU, and U.S. reforms, including MiFID II, CSDR, benchmark transition, Basel III, intermediate parent companies, and climate-risk supervision.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s global financial-services business, scale, subsidiaries, disclosures, and reporting segments; the competitive landscape and basis of competition; and its human-capital strategy, workforce composition and diversity, culture, inclusion, recruiting, development, compensation, and benefits. It also outlines extensive U.S. and international regulation, covering capital, liquidity, governance, resolution, banking and consumer protections, securities and derivatives, privacy, cybersecurity, financial crime controls, compensation, and evolving regulatory reforms.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
Summary
nodes.summary: The section warns that listed risks, alone or together, could materially harm JPMorgan Chase’s finances, operations, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation, and that the list is not exhaustive. It summarizes risks involving COVID-19; regulation and legal matters; politics, markets, credit, liquidity and capital; operations, strategy, conduct and reputation; countries; and employees. It details how the pandemic disrupted markets, supply chains and businesses, reduced demand and increased credit-loss allowances, and how prolonged or worsening effects could cause further losses, valuation changes, rating downgrades, liquidity or capital constraints, workforce disruption, and scrutiny over government-program participation. Outcomes depend on uncertain health, policy and economic developments. It also explains that extensive, changing global financial regulation can raise costs, restrict or reshape business, and affect products, market-making, investments, taxes and ESG or competition-related activities.

nodes.title: Differences in financial services regulation can be disadvantageous for JPMorgan Chase’s businesses.
Differences in financial services regulation can be disadvantageous for JPMorgan Chase’s businesses. (intro)
nodes.summary: Differences in financial regulation may disadvantage JPMorgan Chase relative to larger, more heavily regulated firms, less-regulated fintech and other competitors, or institutions favored by local rules, potentially costing market share. Implementation of global standards also varies across jurisdictions, sometimes adding stricter requirements. Foreign initiatives may require changes to local entities and operations, including rules on capital and liquidity, ring-fencing, resolution, transaction clearing, derivatives, governance, conduct, controls, and compensation. Regulatory inconsistencies may force divestitures or restructuring, raise costs, change prices, limit products and business opportunities, and ultimately weaken competitiveness, results, and profitability.

nodes.title: Resolving regulatory investigations can subject JPMorgan Chase to significant penalties and collateral consequences, and could result in higher compliance costs or restrictions on its operations.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces heightened regulatory scrutiny, investigations, penalties, remediation costs, and operational restrictions. Admissions or criminal resolutions may increase litigation and reputational risks, cost clients, limit products or jurisdictions, or threaten business permissions. The bank expects formal enforcement to continue and may face harsher action due to prior investigations; failures to meet resolutions or control standards could trigger further penalties, restrictions, prosecution, or litigation. Global AML, sanctions, embargo, and anti-corruption rules raise compliance costs and conflict-of-law risks. Unpredictable legal systems abroad may undermine operations and earnings. Resolution-plan requirements could force restructuring, raise costs, limit services, or—if plans have deficiencies—lead to stricter capital, leverage, liquidity, growth, or business constraints.

nodes.title: Regulatory Compliance and Jurisdictional Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase can face greater risks of non-compliance and incur higher operational and compliance costs under laws, rules and regulations relating to anti-money laundering, economic sanctions, embargo programs and anti-corruption.
JPMorgan Chase’s operations and financial results can be negatively impacted in countries with less predictable legal and regulatory frameworks.
nodes.summary: Prior investigations or enforcement actions may increase the likelihood of further regulatory action. Failing to meet resolution terms or heightened control standards can lead to additional settlements, penalties, business restrictions, sanctions, prosecution, or civil litigation. Global anti-money laundering, sanctions, embargo, and anti-corruption requirements raise compliance costs and non-compliance risks, including from conflicting laws. In countries with unpredictable legal systems, ambiguous rules, weak contract enforcement, government control, corruption, or arbitrary proceedings can disrupt operations, require added resources, reduce earnings, and make compliance harder.

nodes.title: Requirements for the orderly resolution of JPMorgan Chase could result in JPMorgan Chase having to restructure or reorganize its businesses and could increase its funding or operational costs or curtail its businesses.
nodes.summary: Federal Reserve and FDIC rules require JPMorgan Chase to periodically submit plans for rapid, orderly bankruptcy resolution without extraordinary government support. Changes in agency assessments or requirements could force changes to its structure or activities, raising costs or limiting service to customers. If both agencies find plan deficiencies, they may impose stricter capital, leverage or liquidity requirements, restrict growth or operations, or require restructuring, reorganization or divestitures that could materially harm its operations and strategy.

nodes.title: Holders of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s debt and equity securities will absorb losses if it were to enter into a resolution.
nodes.summary: Federal Reserve rules require JPMorgan Chase’s parent to maintain eligible long-term debt to recapitalize subsidiaries in resolution. Under its preferred single-point-of-entry strategy, the parent alone enters bankruptcy; equity absorbs losses first, then unsecured creditors, whose claims rank behind subsidiary creditors and the parent’s secured and statutory-priority creditors. The FDIC has considered, but not formally adopted, a similar Title II approach; no authority is bound to JPMorgan’s plan, and creditor losses could be greater. Political uncertainty—including monetary and fiscal policy, pandemic responses, isolationism, conflict, sanctions, tariffs, and other government actions—may disrupt markets and growth, weaken confidence in the dollar, heighten international tensions, reduce support for U.S. housing GSEs, raise government funding and debt-service concerns, or cause shutdowns.

nodes.title: Economic uncertainty or instability caused by political developments can negatively impact JPMorgan Chase’s businesses.
nodes.summary: The text explains that in a JPMorgan Chase resolution, Parent Company equity holders and then unsecured creditors—including eligible long-term debt holders—may absorb losses, behind subsidiary, secured, and statutory-priority creditors; the preferred single-point-of-entry approach is not guaranteed, and Title II adoption remains uncertain. It also outlines how political uncertainty and adverse economic or market conditions can disrupt growth, markets, credit, confidence, clients, and government support, causing losses, liquidity or capital declines, and operational constraints. Risks include geopolitical conflict, policy shifts, sanctions, tariffs, pandemics, cyberattacks, climate events, market volatility, and consumer economic pressures such as unemployment, housing, inflation, and debt.

nodes.title: Economic and market events and conditions can materially affect JPMorgan Chase’s businesses and investment and market-making positions.
nodes.summary: Political, economic and market disruptions can alter investor behavior, confidence in government support, counterparties’ financial health, and JPMorgan Chase’s business decisions. They may trigger recession or inflation, volatility, tighter credit, asset repricing, debt and securities selloffs, reduced activity, currency or alliance changes, expropriation, and contagion. Adverse sentiment, labor, capital, interest-rate, price, geopolitical, cyber, climate, disaster, health or other conditions can harm results. Unexpected asset declines, credit events, changing correlations, ineffective hedging or unpriced risks may cause portfolio and market-making losses, weakening profitability, liquidity and capital and constraining business growth and services.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s consumer businesses can be negatively affected by adverse economic conditions and governmental policies.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s consumer businesses face risks from economic conditions—including income distribution, unemployment, low interest rates, housing prices, inflation, confidence, spending and consumer debt. Reduced incomes, weak growth, recession or inflation may lower demand and worsen delinquencies, credit-loss allowances and charge-offs, reducing earnings; impacts may be greater in affected industries or regions and among customers with high debt, such as student loans. Government policies on healthcare, education, immigration, employment and housing, as well as higher taxes and regulation, may reduce consumer income or demand. Allowing student loans to be discharged in bankruptcy could encourage bankruptcies and defaults on credit cards and other consumer loans.

nodes.title: Unfavorable market and economic conditions can have an adverse effect on JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale businesses.
nodes.summary: Adverse market and economic conditions can reduce JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale transaction volumes, client participation, and fee revenue, while forcing losses on unsold credit commitments and harming clients in stressed sectors, potentially causing credit losses. Falling asset values, higher rates, fund outflows, or shifts to lower-revenue products can reduce asset-management and custody fees and trigger performance-damaging asset sales and further withdrawals. Economic downturns and spending changes can also weaken wholesale clients, especially commercial real estate borrowers, reducing rents and property values, impairing debt service and refinancing, and increasing credit-loss allowances, delinquencies, defaults, charge-offs, and servicing costs.

nodes.title: Market, Interest Rate and Counterparty Risks
key_items: Changes in interest rates and credit spreads can adversely affect certain of JPMorgan Chase’s revenue and income streams related to its traditional banking and funding activities.
JPMorgan Chase’s results may be materially affected by market fluctuations and significant changes in the value of financial instruments.
nodes.summary: Explains how low, negative, or rising interest rates and changing credit spreads can affect JPMorgan Chase’s margins, deposits, lending, securities, mortgage servicing rights, funding costs, liquidity, capital, and borrower repayment. Market volatility and illiquidity can make financial instruments difficult to value or sell and cause losses, while risk controls and hedges may fail in extreme events. Client, counterparty, custodian, or clearinghouse defaults or failures can also cause losses, disputes, litigation, and contract-replacement costs.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase can be negatively affected by adverse changes in the financial condition of clients, counterparties, custodians and CCPs.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s exposure to interest-rate, credit-spread, market-valuation and counterparty risks. Low or negative rates can compress margins, alter deposit behavior, reduce deposits and diminish mortgage-servicing-rights values; widening spreads raise borrowing costs and affect fair-valued liabilities. Rising rates may boost net interest income but also reduce loan originations, cause underwriting and securities losses, prompt deposit outflows, create pricing mismatches, reduce liquidity, increase funding costs and impair variable-rate loan payments—harming earnings, liquidity or capital. Market volatility and illiquidity can make instruments difficult to value or sell, while ineffective hedging may amplify losses despite stress testing. Defaults or failures involving clients, counterparties, custodians, CCPs or government entities may cause credit losses, replacement and operational costs, litigation, regulatory scrutiny, disputes, reputational harm, or impediments to resolving claims; inadequate collateral and legal or sovereign risks can worsen outcomes. Failure of a major market participant may trigger cascading market disruption and losses.

The section describes regulatory, resolution, political, economic, market, interest-rate and counterparty risks to JPMorgan Chase. Divergent rules, investigations, enforcement, compliance duties and resolution-plan requirements can raise costs, restrict or restructure operations, and weaken competitiveness. In resolution, parent equity and then unsecured creditors may absorb losses. Political and economic disruption can affect markets, confidence, clients, consumers and government support. Downturns may reduce consumer and wholesale demand, increase defaults and credit losses, and lower fees. Rate changes, volatility, illiquidity, failed hedges and client or market-participant defaults can impair earnings, liquidity, capital and growth.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase may suffer losses if the value of collateral declines in stressed market conditions.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase may incur losses when collateral values decline during stressed or illiquid markets. Credit risk can rise if it cannot realize collateral’s fair value, liquidation proceeds fail to cover amounts owed, or counterparties cannot post collateral for operational or other reasons. Increased valuation disputes in volatile markets may also lead to losses if the firm cannot realize fair value or manage collateral declines.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase could incur significant losses arising from concentrations of credit and market risk.
JPMorgan Chase could incur significant losses arising from concentrations of credit and market risk. (intro)
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s risks from concentrated credit and market exposures among connected clients, industries, or regions, including contagion, fair-value losses, and regulator-driven credit-loss allowances; consumer-loan competition and defaults; and difficulty reducing positions during market disruptions, which can raise risk-weighted assets, weaken capital, increase funding costs, and reduce profitability. Liquidity can be strained by market disruption, unexpected outflows or requirements, asset-sale limits, participant defaults, and lost confidence, forcing costly alternative funding and potentially constraining operations. Finally, the holding company depends on subsidiary cash flows to meet obligations; regulatory and internal limits on bank and IHC payments may restrict its ability to pay interest on debt.

nodes.title: Consumer Credit Risks and Liquidity Constraints
key_items: JPMorgan Chase’s ability to operate its businesses could be impaired if its liquidity is constrained.
nodes.summary: Consumer credit losses may rise if concentrated exposures, competitive lending, weaker borrower standards, defaults, or recession impair repayment; unsuccessful hedging or inability to reduce positions during market disruption may increase risk-weighted assets, weaken capital, raise funding costs, and reduce profitability. Liquidity can be constrained by market disruption, unforeseen requirements, asset-sale difficulties, counterparty defaults, unexpected cash or collateral outflows, deposit losses, increased commitment draws, or declining confidence. Stress may raise funding costs and limit traditional funding access, forcing more expensive or scarce alternatives. Regulatory liquidity ratios, resolution plans, and foreign requirements to pre-position liquidity may also increase costs; poor liquidity management could restrict funding and investment in businesses and subsidiaries and harm results.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a holding company and depends on the cash flows of its subsidiaries to make payments on its outstanding securities.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a holding company that relies on subsidiaries for cash flows. It owns JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and the IHC, which holds most other subsidiaries, other assets, and lends to the holding company. The holding company must contribute substantially all securities-issuance proceeds to the IHC. Bank and IHC payments to the holding company are constrained by regulatory, capital, liquidity, management, and board limits. Consequently, limited subsidiary dividends and IHC borrowings could impair the holding company’s ability to pay debt interest, equity dividends, redeem or repurchase securities, and meet other obligations, potentially prompting earlier bankruptcy protection or resolution.

nodes.title: Reductions in JPMorgan Chase’s credit ratings may adversely affect its liquidity and cost of funding.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase and certain subsidiaries are rated based on factors including profitability, risk management, legal expenses, subsidiary rating differences, regulation, government support, and economic and geopolitical conditions. Despite monitoring these factors, downgrades remain possible, particularly during market instability. Lower ratings could restrict business, reduce profitability and market access, raise securities and funding costs, trigger collateral requirements, deter investors and counterparties, increase credit spreads, and reduce the value of the company’s debt and other obligations.

nodes.title: The reform and replacement of benchmark rates could adversely affect financial instruments issued, funded, serviced or held by JPMorgan Chase and expose it to litigation and other disputes.
nodes.summary: Benchmark reforms—including changes to administration, restrictions, replacement rates and contract amendments—may disrupt markets, alter or discontinue benchmarks, increase compliance and operating costs, discourage benchmark contributions, cause reputational harm, and adversely affect the value, returns and markets for JPMorgan Chase-linked financial instruments. Alternative rates may not be economically equivalent, effective or widely accepted. LIBOR’s principal U.S. dollar tenors are scheduled to cease after June 30, 2023, with SOFR intended as a replacement; inadequate acceptance or transition arrangements could cause market dislocation, pricing volatility and reduced capital-market activity, harming JPMorgan Chase and its instruments. The transition may also prompt client, customer, counterparty or investor disputes alleging unfair treatment or losses, inadequate communication or conflict disclosure, unsuitable recommendations or products, anticompetitive conduct or manipulation, or unfavorable contract interpretation. Litigation could raise costs, require substantial payments and damage reputation.

nodes.title: Capital
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s ability to support business, meet regulatory requirements, and return capital to shareholders may be affected by maintaining required capital levels and composition. As a GSIB, it faces leverage- and risk-based requirements and additional buffers—the GSIB surcharge, SCB, and countercyclical buffer—reassessed at least annually. Requirements may rise due to regulatory changes; government or Federal Reserve responses to systemic events, such as pandemic measures that increased deposits, leverage exposure, and the GSIB surcharge; or balance-sheet changes and developments that raise risk-weighted assets, including greater market risk, customer delinquencies, and client downgrades.

nodes.title: Maintaining the required level and composition of capital may impact JPMorgan Chase’s ability to support business activities, meet evolving regulatory requirements and distribute capital to shareholders.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from discontinuing financial benchmarks: replacement rates may not be economically equivalent, effectively implemented, or widely accepted. A failed transition from U.S. dollar LIBOR to SOFR could disrupt markets, increase volatility, suppress capital-market activity, and harm JPMorgan Chase and related instruments. The transition may also prompt client, counterparty, or investor disputes over unfair treatment, disclosure, recommendations, anti-competitive conduct, or contract interpretation, raising costs and reputational risk. It then explains that regulatory, leverage- and risk-based capital requirements and GSIB buffers may rise because of regulatory actions, systemic events, balance-sheet or risk changes, or higher stress losses. Insufficient capital or stricter requirements could limit buybacks, affect capital instruments and dividends, and constrain business activities.

nodes.title: Operational
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase relies on accurate, secure, continuously functioning operational systems, careful maintenance and upgrades, and systems run by vendors and other market participants. Disruptions—including malfunctions and cyberbreaches—could delay services, liquidity, information, settlement, or access to assets; cause erroneous transactions, losses, higher costs, customer dissatisfaction, sanctions, diminished confidence, and reputational harm. Growing transaction speed, volume, connectivity, and complexity heighten risks from fraud, widespread or compounding errors, software or hardware failures, and intellectual-property claims against key technology. The passage ends mid-sentence while discussing systems of acquired businesses and external parties.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s businesses are dependent on the effectiveness of its operational systems and those of other market participants.
nodes.summary: Higher Federal Reserve stress-loss estimates or failure to meet capital requirements could raise JPMorgan Chase’s SCB and constrain share repurchases, capital instrument actions, dividends, or business operations. Its businesses depend on reliable internal and third-party operational systems, accurate data, secure maintenance and upgrades, and external providers such as clearing, payment, cloud, and technology firms. System failures, cyberattacks, errors, or disruptions could delay services and settlements, cause erroneous transactions and losses, increase costs, trigger regulatory sanctions, damage customer confidence and reputation, and disrupt markets. Growing transaction speed, volume, complexity, and interconnectivity heighten risks from fraud, cascading errors, software or hardware failures, and intellectual-property claims. Inadequate systems at JPMorgan Chase, acquired businesses, or external parties could materially harm the firm.

nodes.title: A successful cyber attack affecting JPMorgan Chase could cause significant harm to JPMorgan Chase and its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s cyber and broader operational risks. Frequent attacks from varied actors may steal, manipulate, destroy or expose data, disrupt services, extort money, or enable fraud; past and future breaches are unavoidable risks, difficult to anticipate or contain, and may cause financial, legal, regulatory, reputational and customer harm, with investigations delaying full assessment and response. Risk grows with digital expansion, acquisitions, remote work and third-party connectivity. New products, platforms or business changes may introduce uncontrolled operational risks. Failures or breaches at vendors, customers and financial-market infrastructure can raise fraud, remediation costs and dissatisfaction, require protective access restrictions, and trigger industry-wide disruption.

nodes.title: Cyber and Operational Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase can be negatively affected if it fails to identify and address operational risks associated with the introduction of or changes to products, services and delivery platforms.
JPMorgan Chase’s operational costs and customer satisfaction could be adversely affected by the failure of an external operational system.
nodes.summary: Cyberattacks may take time to investigate and contain, allowing harm to spread, delaying reliable disclosure, and increasing costs. New or changed products, services, platforms, and business investments can create unmanaged operational risks, potentially causing liability, expenses, litigation, reputational or liquidity damage, regulatory action, and weaker competitiveness. Failures or breaches at connected vendors, market infrastructure, customers, and other external parties can enable fraud, losses, remediation costs, and reputational harm; protective measures may raise costs and reduce customer confidence. Growing interconnectivity also creates risk of industry-wide disruption.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase’s operations rely on its ability, and the ability of key external parties, to maintain appropriately-staffed workforces, and on the competence, trustworthiness, health and safety of employees.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase depends on appropriately staffed, competent, trustworthy, and safe employees, as well as the workforces of vendors and other external parties, to operate efficiently, serve customers, and manage risk. Its businesses may be harmed by poor execution of decisions, inadequate risk controls or training, labor shortages, operational failures, theft, fraud, unlawful conduct, human error, or misconduct. Operations may also be impaired if the company, government authorities, or external parties fail to protect employee health and safety effectively.

JPMorgan Chase faces concentrated credit and market risks, consumer defaults, difficulty exiting positions, liquidity pressures, and reliance on subsidiary cash flows, with potential losses, higher funding costs, and constraints on payments. Credit-rating downgrades and benchmark-rate reforms may disrupt funding and markets, reduce instrument values, and prompt disputes or litigation. Capital rules and buffers may increase, limiting business growth and shareholder distributions. Operational risks include system failures, cyberattacks, fraud, third-party and market-infrastructure disruptions, technology and transition risks, and inadequate staffing, employee competence, conduct, or safety—potentially causing financial, regulatory, customer, and reputational harm.

nodes.title: JPMorgan Chase faces substantial legal and operational risks in safeguarding personal information.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s risks from privacy laws and data breaches; extraordinary disruptions and limits of its resiliency plans; vendor oversight failures; weaknesses in risk management, data, models, estimates and judgments, including effects on capital and regulatory approval; and disclosure or financial-reporting control failures. It also covers strategic execution risks, competition from banks and technology and nonbank firms, evolving technologies and cryptocurrencies, and resulting pressures on customers, revenues, costs, market share, reputation, and financial condition.

nodes.title: The effects of climate change could adversely impact JPMorgan Chase and its clients.
nodes.summary: Climate change may financially affect JPMorgan Chase and its clients through acute and chronic physical hazards and the transition to a low-carbon economy. Physical impacts include asset losses, reduced insurance, operational and supply-chain disruptions, and economic or demographic shifts; transition impacts include stranded assets, higher costs, business-model changes, and reputational harm. These risks can weaken clients’ finances and creditworthiness. The text also describes conduct risk: despite policies and training, employee misconduct may harm customers, markets, and the firm. Examples include improper sales, trading or fraud, tax-related transactions, fiduciary or competition violations, unauthorized communications, discrimination, poor risk management, and misappropriation. Resulting proceedings may bring losses, penalties, added costs, oversight, restrictions, customer attrition, and reputational damage; risks may rise when integrating acquired businesses.

nodes.title: Reputation Damage to JPMorgan Chase’s reputation could harm its businesses.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s risks from reputational damage, including misconduct, security and operational failures, legal or regulatory issues, adverse publicity, activism over sensitive-sector clients, industry practices, conflicts of interest and fiduciary failures, and their effects on business, employees, customers, investors and costs. It describes risks from international conflict, cyberattacks, and countries’ economic, political, regulatory and social instability. It also covers competition for diverse talent and restrictive immigration policies; litigation and government investigations; and annual-report disclosures on unresolved comments, headquarters and property holdings, legal proceedings, mine safety, facilities and possible costs of disposing of excess space.

JPMorgan Chase’s non-exhaustive risk factors could materially harm its finances, operations, capital, liquidity, competitiveness, or reputation. They include COVID-19 and economic uncertainty; changing and divergent regulation, resolution, legal proceedings, and political, country, market, interest-rate, counterparty, credit, collateral, concentration, funding, liquidity, capital, and benchmark-rate risks; climate impacts; and operational, cyber, privacy, vendor, resilience, data, model, reporting-control, technology, strategy, competition, and cryptocurrency risks. The section also addresses employee, conduct, talent, and reputational risks, including misconduct, conflicts, sensitive-sector activity, international instability, and disclosure matters, and explains potential losses, restrictions, costs, enforcement, customer attrition, and other harm.

nodes.title: Staff Comments, Properties, and Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: There are no unresolved staff comments. JPMorgan Chase owns its 47-story headquarters at 383 Madison Avenue in New York City; demolition of its former 270 Park Avenue headquarters was completed in 2021, and construction of a new headquarters there has begun. See pages 52–54 for occupancy expense information and Note 30 for material legal proceedings.

nodes.title: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures.
key_items: Parts I and II; Item 2. Properties.
nodes.summary: Mine safety disclosures are not applicable. The text lists the Firm’s owned or leased facilities at year-end 2021 by U.S., EMEA, and Asia-Pacific/Latin America/Canada locations, totaling 73.8 million square feet, and notes 4,790 retail branches across 48 states and Washington, D.C. Facilities serve all business segments and corporate needs; excess-property disposals may be uncertain and costly. It describes the NYSE listing, shareholder and dividend references, and the history and regulatory limits of the 2021 $30 billion share-repurchase authorization, with quarterly and year-to-date repurchase figures. Item 6 is reserved; Item 7 directs readers to management’s discussion and analysis and the financial statements.

summary: Part I describes JPMorgan Chase’s global businesses, subsidiaries, reporting segments, competitive position, workforce and human-capital practices, and extensive regulatory environment. nodes.title: Explanation and Reconciliation of the Firm's Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures

Managed results reclassify revenue to a fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) basis, making taxable and tax-exempt sources comparable; related tax effects are recorded in tax expense and do not change net income. Other non-GAAP measures help assess operational performance, trends, and competitors, but may differ from similarly named measures elsewhere. A table reconciles reported to managed results for 2019–2021, including revenue, expenses, pre-provision profit, credit-loss provisions, pretax income, taxes, net income, and overhead ratios. A reconciliation reports period-end and annual average common equity, goodwill, other intangibles, qualifying deferred tax liabilities and resulting TCE, plus ROTCE and TBVPS where applicable, for 2019–2021. nodes.title: Firmwide Risk Management
Risk governance and oversight framework
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its firmwide approach to balancing client and investor service with safety and soundness, emphasizing individual responsibility, business-level risk ownership, governance, and risk-aware compensation. Its framework considers risk drivers, four types (strategic, credit and investment, market, and operational), and quantitative and qualitative impacts. Independent Risk Management, led by the CRO under Board Risk Committee oversight, sets and oversees governance. The three defense lines are business units, independent Risk Management, and Internal Audit; supporting functions also contribute. Businesses identify and control risks, while IRM reviews and consolidates them. Senior management and the Board Risk Committee set and monitor quantitative and qualitative risk appetite.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight structure
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Firm’s independent risk management governance and escalation structure, including the Operating Committee’s reporting to the Board. It describes Board and bank-board oversight, with committee responsibilities for risk, controls and audit, compensation and culture, public responsibility, and corporate governance. It summarizes senior management committees overseeing firmwide risk and controls, business and regional risks, asset-liability management, and valuation. nodes.title: Strategic Risk Management
Management and oversight
nodes.summary: Strategic risk is the potential harm to earnings, capital, liquidity, or reputation from flawed business plans or inadequate responses to operating changes. The Operating Committee and business and corporate leaders manage major risks; IRM oversees them through reviews and governance forums, while the Board and Board Risk Committee provide oversight. Leaders identify initiative risks and appetite impacts, and IRM assesses effects on the Firm’s risk profile. Periodically updated strategic plans evaluate performance, the operating environment, and strategies; initiatives and assessments feed the budget and Board approval. Balance-sheet strategy emphasizes risk-adjusted returns, capital strength, and liquidity, with related sections covering capital, liquidity, and reputation risks.

nodes.title: Capital Risk Management
Governance
nodes.summary: The text defines capital risk as inadequate capital level or composition under normal and stressed conditions, and describes the Firm’s strategy of maintaining a strong, liquid balance sheet and considering capital impacts in major decisions. It outlines independent Capital Management Oversight duties: monitoring metrics, limits, appetite and breaches, assessing capital management and contingency planning, and reviewing regulatory compliance. Treasury & CIO manages capital to support investment, flexibility, subsidiaries, regulatory standards, distributions, and resolution readiness through internal requirements, governance, and monitoring. Oversight involves several management committees and periodic Board Risk Committee review.

nodes.title: Capital planning and stress testing

nodes.title: Paycheck Protection Program
nodes.summary: A September 2020 final rule assigned PPP loans a zero percent risk weight to neutralize their effect on risk-based capital ratios. PPP loans remain in total leverage exposure for SLR purposes because the Firm did not use the Federal Reserve’s facility that would have allowed their exclusion.

Effective April 1, 2021, the rule had no material impact on the Firm’s risk-based capital metrics.

nodes.title: Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk
nodes.summary: In November 2019, U.S. banking regulators adopted SA-CCR, replacing the current exposure method for derivatives counterparty exposure in Standardized RWA and leverage exposure in the SLR framework. It applies to Basel III Advanced Approaches organizations, including JPMorgan Chase, starting January 1, 2022. Based on December 31, 2021 derivatives exposure, adoption was estimated to increase the Firm’s Standardized RWA by about $40 billion and modestly decrease total leverage exposure; actual effects could vary with exposure composition as of March 31, 2022.

nodes.title: Risk-based Capital Regulatory Requirements

nodes.title: Capital Surcharges, TLAC, and Leverage Requirements

nodes.summary: The page reports the Firm’s GSIB surcharges: 2022 Method 1 and 2 rates remain 2.0% and 3.5%, with increases projected for 2023 and 2024 based on later calculations. The countercyclical buffer was 0% at year-end 2021; regulators may raise it by up to 2.5%, and capital shortfalls can restrict distributions and bonuses. The Firm expects a near-term CET1 ratio of 12%–13%. Federal Reserve rules require minimum external TLAC and eligible long-term debt. The SLR minimum is 3%, plus a 2% buffer for the Firm; its calculation includes on- and certain off-balance-sheet exposures, and falling short limits distributions and bonuses.
