It presents SLR components and ratios (6.9% in 2021; 5.4% in 2020, or 5.8% excluding relief), and describes capital-allocation methods, their 2022 update and 2023 GSIB surcharge, and allocated equity by business segment for 2020–2022.

nodes.title: Line of business equity
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021 Basel III Standardized and Advanced RWA rollforwards by credit, market, and operational risk, with estimated drivers including model/data changes, portfolio runoff, and portfolio movements; it defines these drivers, gives off-balance-sheet credit RWA figures for 2020–2021, and points to Pillar 3 disclosures. It presents SLR components and ratios for 2021 and 2020, explains calculation adjustments and prior-year relief, and references Note 27. It also describes capital allocation and ROE performance measures, the 2022 allocation methodology changes reflecting RWA and a future 4.0% GSIB surcharge, and allocated equity by business segment for 2022, 2021, and 2020.

nodes.title: Capital actions
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Firm’s capital actions. Common dividends are governed by its capital-management framework, currently $1.00 per share quarterly with Board approval; payout ratios were 25% in 2021, 40% in 2020 and 31% in 2019, subject to restrictions. After Federal Reserve restrictions, the Firm resumed repurchases in 2021 under a Board-authorized program of up to $30 billion; temporary limits expired June 30, after the Firm passed the 2021 CCAR stress test. Repurchases totaled 119.7 million shares ($18.448 billion) in 2021, 50.0 million ($6.397 billion) in 2020 and 213.0 million ($24.121 billion) in 2019. The 2020 program was suspended amid COVID-19 and regulatory direction. Management controls timing and volume based on market, regulatory, capital and investment factors; purchases may use open markets, private transactions or Rule 10b5-1 plans, and can be suspended. Preferred dividends were $1.6 billion in 2021; the Firm issued and redeemed several non-cumulative series and redeemed $2.0 billion of Series Z on February 1, 2022, following its December 2021 announcement.

nodes.title: Other capital requirements
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve’s TLAC rule requires U.S. GSIB holding companies, including JPMorgan Chase, to maintain minimum external total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) and eligible long-term debt (LTD). Falling below requirements plus buffers restricts capital distributions and certain executive bonuses. A table reports 2021 and 2020 eligible TLAC and LTD amounts, ratios to risk-weighted assets (RWA) and leverage exposure, regulatory minimums, and surpluses or shortfalls, reflecting CECL transition provisions. RWA uses the greater of standardized and advanced measures; leverage exposure excludes U.S. Treasury securities and Federal Reserve deposits during the specified temporary rule period. The text directs readers to further information on GSIB surcharges, Parent Company long-term debt, and resolution-related consequences for debt and equity holders.

nodes.title: Broker-dealer regulatory capital
nodes.summary: J.P. Morgan Securities, JPMorgan Chase’s principal U.S. broker-dealer and a registered futures commission merchant, is subject to SEC, CFTC, FINRA and NFA capital rules and uses the Net Capital Rule’s alternative method. At December 31, 2021, its net capital was $24.581 billion versus a $5.968 billion minimum. Following its November 2021 registration as a security-based swap dealer, it faced higher tentative-net-capital thresholds; it met the $5 billion minimum and $6 billion notification threshold. J.P. Morgan Securities plc, a wholly owned subsidiary regulated by the U.K. PRA and FCA, is subject to U.K.-implemented EU capital rules and Basel III. It complied with fully phased-in MREL requirements at year-end 2021. Its capital metrics were $54.818 billion in total capital, a CET1 ratio of 18.5% versus a 4.5% minimum, and a total capital ratio of 23.7% versus an 8.0% minimum; ratios also exceeded PRA requirements including buffers.

Covers capital-risk governance, oversight, balance-sheet strategy, annual capital planning, ICAAP, stress testing, contingency actions, and COVID-19 resilience. Describes Basel III risk-based, leverage, GSIB surcharge, TLAC, eligible-debt, and well-capitalized requirements, including CECL transition, PPP treatment, TLAC holdings, and SA-CCR. Reports capital components, rollforwards, RWA and SLR metrics, allocation methods and business-line equity, dividends, share repurchases, preferred-stock actions, and regulatory capital disclosures. Also details U.S. and U.K. broker-dealer capital rules, compliance, and reported capital levels.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk Management
Liquidity Risk Management and Governance
nodes.summary: Defines liquidity risk and describes Liquidity Risk Oversight’s independent monitoring, limits, reporting, stress testing, process reviews, and assumption approvals or escalations. Treasury & CIO manages liquidity to support businesses and obligations through normal and stressed conditions and optimize funding, using asset-liability analysis, stress assumptions, strategies, contingency plans, risk limits, regulatory compliance, and liquidity-based FTP. A centralized global approach optimizes liquidity, monitors exposures and transfer constraints, and maintains appropriate surplus. Governance involves Firmwide, business-line and regional ALCOs, the Treasurer Committee, CTC Risk Committee, and Board Risk Committee review and approval recommendations.

nodes.title: Internal stress testing
nodes.summary: The Firm regularly stress-tests liquidity for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and material legal entities, including resolution and recovery scenarios, and runs additional tests for specific market events or concerns. Tests assume contractual obligations are met and assess funding-market access, contingent outflows, and restrictions on moving liquidity across jurisdictions and entities, across time horizons, currencies, and market or idiosyncratic stresses. Results inform funding plans and liquidity assessments. The Parent Company funds the Firm through equity and long-term debt, while the IHC supports the Parent Company and subsidiaries. Liquidity is maintained across these entities to meet tolerances and minimums and withstand disrupted funding.

nodes.title: Contingency funding plan
nodes.summary:
Contingency funding plan
The Firm’s Contingency Funding Plan (“CFP”) sets out the strategies for addressing and managing liquidity resource needs during a liquidity stress event and incorporates liquidity risk limits, indicators and risk appetite tolerances. The CFP also identifies the alternative contingent funding and liquidity resources available to the Firm and its legal entities in a period of stress.

nodes.title: Liquidity Coverage Ratio and HQLA
nodes.summary: The LCR rule requires JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to hold eligible, unencumbered high-quality liquid assets sufficient for 30 days of stressed net outflows, with a minimum LCR of 100%. Bank excess HQLA that cannot be transferred to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s LCR. The table reports average LCR, HQLA, outflows and excess liquidity for the three months ended December 2021, September 2021 and December 2020; the Firm’s LCR was 111%, 112% and 110%, and the Bank’s was 178%, 174% and 160%. Firm LCR rose year over year mainly due to long-term debt issuance; Bank LCR rose due to deposit growth. Ratios fluctuate with HQLA and outflows; disclosure reports are available on the Firm’s website.

nodes.title: Other liquidity sources
nodes.summary: Beyond eligible HQLA, the Firm held unencumbered marketable securities, including excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that cannot be transferred to non-bank affiliates. Their fair value was $914 billion at year-end 2021, up from $740 billion in 2020, mainly due to increased deposits; realizable liquidity depends on market conditions. Collateral-backed borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window was about $308 billion and $307 billion, respectively, excluding certain HQLA and pledged securities. The Firm does not consider discount-window or other central-bank borrowing a primary liquidity source.

nodes.title: NSFR
nodes.summary: The NSFR measures large banks’ available stable funding against required funding over one year. A final rule issued October 20, 2020, requires the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to maintain at least 100% on an ongoing basis; it took effect July 1, 2021. The Firm must begin semiannual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR in 2023. As of December 31, 2021, both entities complied with the minimum, based on the Firm’s understanding of the rule.

nodes.title: Funding
Funding Sources of funds
nodes.summary: Management says secured and unsecured funding is sufficient for short- and long-term on- and off-balance-sheet needs. The Firm uses deposits, capital-market borrowing and equity; banks rely mainly on deposits, while non-bank subsidiaries use long-term unsecured and short-term secured funding. Excess funds go to securities, cash or other liquid investments. Deposit tables compare period-end and average balances by business line for 2021 and 2020. Deposits, especially consumer and wholesale operating deposits, provide stable liquidity; insurance can add stability and benefit the LCR. Estimated uninsured deposits were $1,489.6 billion in 2021 versus $1,275.9 billion in 2020, primarily wholesale operating deposits. Tables detail estimated uninsured U.S. and non-U.S. time deposits by maturity and report deposits, loans, loans-to-deposits ratios and deposits as a share of liabilities: deposits rose from $2,144.3 billion to $2,462.3 billion, loans from $1,012.9 billion to $1,077.7 billion, the ratio fell from 47% to 44%, and the liability share rose from 69% to 71%.

nodes.title: Deposits
nodes.summary: Management says diversified secured and unsecured funding, deposits, capital-market borrowings and equity are sufficient for obligations; excess funds are invested in securities or liquid assets. The text details deposit balances by business segment for 2021–2020, their stability and insurance benefits, uninsured deposits and time-deposit maturities, loans-to-deposits ratios, and trends in average deposits. It also provides U.S. and non-U.S. deposit balances and interest rates for 2019–2021, explains pandemic-related inflows and CCB growth, and points to further disclosures on deposits and non-deposit funding.

nodes.title: Sources of funds (excluding deposits)
nodes.summary: The table presents year-end and average funding sources, excluding deposits, in millions for 2021 and 2020. It details short- and long-term unsecured and secured funding, including commercial paper, borrowings, federal funds, repurchase agreements, securities lending, conduit obligations, notes, securitizations, FHLB advances, preferred stock, and common equity. Footnotes explain categories, balance-sheet treatment, TLAC-eligible and secured structured notes, references for equity details, and nonrecourse Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility advances.

nodes.title: Short-term funding
nodes.summary: The Firm’s short-term secured funding mainly comprises securities lending and repurchase agreements backed largely by high-quality government and agency securities; repo balances fell in 2021 because of lower financing of investment securities and trading assets, and balances fluctuate with client activity, financing needs, liability management, and market factors. Short-term unsecured funding includes commercial paper and other borrowings: commercial paper rose for liquidity management, while other borrowings increased due mainly to structured-note issuance. Long-term funding supports stable liquidity and is planned around client activity, liquidity, regulation including TLAC, diversification, market access, cost, markets, maturities, and currencies. Most long-term unsecured debt is issued by the Parent Company, with proceeds advanced to the IHC, which issues no external debt. Tables report 2021 and 2020 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by instrument and entity, and secured credit-card securitization, FHLB advances, and other secured funding. Client-driven loan securitizations are excluded as they do not fund the Firm.

nodes.title: Long-Term Funding and Issuance
nodes.summary: Long-term funding supports stable funding and liquidity, guided by client activity, liquidity needs, and regulations including TLAC. The Firm diversifies markets, tenors, and currencies to preserve market access and optimize costs. Most unsecured debt is issued by the Parent Company, which passes nearly all net proceeds to the IHC; the IHC issues no external debt. The page presents 2021 and 2020 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by entity and debt type, notes TLAC-eligible structured debt, and describes secured funding through credit-card securitizations and FHLB advances, with a table of related activity referenced.

nodes.title: Long-term secured funding
nodes.summary: The table reports 2021 and 2020 long-term secured funding issuance and maturities/redemptions, in millions, across credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, other secured funding, and total funding. Other funding includes secured long-term structured notes. Client-driven loan securitizations by wholesale businesses are excluded because they are not a Firm funding source; see Note 14.

Covers the Firm’s funding strategy, adequacy and sources, including deposits, capital-market borrowing and equity; deposit balances by business, geography and period, stability and insurance benefits, uninsured deposits and maturities, interest rates, loans-to-deposits ratios and pandemic-related trends. It details non-deposit funding balances and instruments, short-term secured and unsecured funding trends, and long-term funding strategy, issuance and maturities by entity and instrument, including TLAC debt, securitizations, FHLB advances and other secured funding, with relevant tables, footnotes and exclusions.

nodes.title: Credit ratings
nodes.summary: Credit ratings affect financing access, liquidity, funding costs, collateral requirements, and counterparties; the Firm says its stress metrics account for downgrade impacts and that it has sufficient liquidity, while noting possible effects on VIE and other commitments. The text lists 2021 ratings for the Parent Company and key subsidiaries and rating-agency outlook changes, and states unsecured debt has no downgrade-triggered acceleration, borrowing limits, or collateral provisions. It identifies factors supporting ratings and those agencies assess. It also defines reputation risk and describes its governance function, policies, oversight, employee responsibilities, sustainability and environmental considerations, potential harms, and escalation of material issues.

Describes the Firm’s liquidity-risk framework, governance, centralized management, monitoring, limits, reporting, stress testing, funding strategies, contingency plans, and regulatory compliance. Covers internal stress scenarios across entities, currencies, and time horizons; LCR and HQLA requirements and results; other liquid assets and borrowing capacity; NSFR rules and compliance; and funding sources, deposits, market borrowing, instruments, maturities, and trends. Also discusses credit ratings’ effects on liquidity and financing, rating outlooks and downgrade protections, and reputation-risk governance, responsibilities, sustainability considerations, potential harms, and escalation.

nodes.title: Reputation Risk Management
nodes.summary: Reputation risk is the possibility that actions or inaction harm perceptions of the Firm’s integrity or competence among stakeholders. The Firm’s function sets governance across business lines and Corporate, maintains policy and standards, and supports consistent identification, escalation, management, and monitoring. Risks can arise from Firm personnel or business partners and cause losses, litigation, fines, or other harm. Employees must consider reputation when evaluating products, transactions, relationships, jurisdictions, processes, and other activities; sustainability, social responsibility, and environmental impacts are also factors. Material issues are escalated as appropriate.

Explains strategic risk, its governance and oversight, how leaders and IRM identify and assess risks, and how periodically updated strategic plans inform budgeting and Board approval. Covers balance-sheet strategy and capital-risk management, including planning, stress testing, regulatory requirements, capital metrics and allocation, shareholder actions, and broker-dealer compliance. Describes liquidity governance, stress scenarios, reserves, funding, regulatory standards, and credit-rating effects. Also details reputation-risk policies, responsibilities, potential sources and impacts, sustainability considerations, and escalation.

nodes.title: Credit and Investment Risk Management
Credit and Investment Risk Management
nodes.summary: Defines credit and investment risk, covering default, credit-profile changes, and investment losses across consumer, wholesale, securities, and bank-deposit exposures. Describes governance and management activities, including policies, monitoring, approvals, concentration limits, underwriting, criticized exposures, loss estimates, and capital management. Explains measurement using default probability, loss severity, and exposure at default; related allowances and capital for potential losses; and stress testing of economic, business, industry, and country scenarios to assess portfolio impacts and inform risk appetite and counterparty decisions.

nodes.title: Stress testing
nodes.summary: The text defines credit and investment risk as default or credit-profile changes and investment principal or return losses. It describes the Firm’s consumer, wholesale, securities, and bank-deposit credit exposures and Credit Risk Management’s responsibilities: policies, portfolio monitoring and approvals, concentration limits, underwriting, credit authorities, troubled exposures, loss estimates, and capital management. Risk measurement uses default probability, loss severity, and exposure at default, with methods tailored to asset and borrower type; estimates inform allowances for loans, commitments, and investment securities, while capital addresses unexpected losses. Stress testing evaluates alternative economic, business, industry, and country scenarios, potential credit migration and losses, and informs risk appetite and counterparty decisions.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and management
nodes.summary: The Firm’s credit-risk framework preserves independent approvals and sets authorities, concentration limits, rating methods, review standards, and distressed-exposure guidance; independent groups validate selected models and assumptions. Consumer risk monitoring tracks delinquencies, trends, and concentrations against expectations, economic forecasts, and benchmarks, informing underwriting and loss estimates. Wholesale risk is reviewed across portfolios, industries, and counterparties, with periodically adjusted, stress-based limits; wrong-way risk is defined. Exposure is mitigated through underwriting, syndication, sales, securitization, derivatives, netting, and collateral. Independent Credit Review validates wholesale risk grades and their timeliness, and assesses credit-management effectiveness, analysis, LGD rationale, monitoring, and policy compliance. Note 12 discusses consumer and wholesale loans.

nodes.title: Risk reporting
nodes.summary: Credit risk reporting supports monitoring and decision-making by regularly informing senior Credit Risk Management of aggregate exposures, forecasts of credit quality, concentrations, and changes in risk profiles. Detailed portfolio reports cover industries, clients, counterparties, customers, products, and geographies. Senior management reviews the adequacy of credit-loss allowances at least quarterly, while risk trends and limit exceptions are regularly shared with and discussed by risk committees, senior management, and the Board of Directors.

nodes.title: Credit Portfolio
nodes.summary: Defines credit risk and the scope of reported credit exposures, with references to related loan, securities, and portfolio disclosures. Presents 2021 and 2020 credit portfolio balances and nonperforming amounts, nonaccrual loans and ratios, and net charge-offs and rates, with notes on exclusions, customer receivables, credit-risk management instruments, and revisions. Describes COVID-19 customer assistance and its potential to delay delinquency recognition. Explains PPP loan terms, accounting, balances, repayments and fee-income effects, program end, and treatment of SBA-guaranteed past-due loans.

nodes.title: Consumer Credit Portfolio
Consumer Credit Portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s retained, primarily prime consumer portfolio, its loan types and mortgage disposition practices, and improved 2021 credit performance. Tables report 2021 and 2020 consumer and credit-card balances, commitments, total exposure, credit-related protection notes, nonaccrual loans, net charge-offs, average retained loans, and charge-off rates. Notes explain portfolio scope, PPP loans and guarantees, available-line commitments, exclusions and COVID-19 deferrals, and calculation details. A maturity and interest-rate table presents 2021 consumer loan maturities and fixed-versus-variable rates, with notes on credit-card TDRs and overdrafts.

nodes.title: Consumer assistance
nodes.summary: Since March 2020, the Firm has provided COVID-19 consumer assistance, mainly payment deferrals. Retained loans in deferral fell from $28.3 billion in June 2020 to $10.7 billion at year-end 2020 and $1.3 billion at year-end 2021; fourth-quarter 2021 enrollments were $386 million, and nearly all borrowers exiting deferral are current. The Firm monitors credit risk and includes expected principal and accrued-interest losses in its allowance. Of year-end 2021 deferrals, $611 million were already TDRs and $40 million became TDRs because they did not qualify for, or were not elected under, temporary CARES Act-related relief, which expired January 1, 2022. Borrowers unable to resume payments will generally enter nonaccrual status and be charged off or written down under Firm policies, subject to the credit-card regulatory exception.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card
Consumer, excluding credit card (intro)
nodes.summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards rose from year-end 2020, as higher residential real estate loans outweighed declines in auto and other loans; Note 12 covers credit quality and delinquencies. The residential portfolio is mainly prime mortgages and HELOCs. Retained loans were flat, nonaccruals declined, and 2021 net recoveries improved; fair-value loans increased while related nonaccruals fell. The text details HELOC balances and risk management, interest-only mortgage balances and terms, government-guaranteed loan delinquencies, and residential portfolio geographic concentrations and improving estimated LTVs.

nodes.title: Modified residential real estate loans
nodes.summary: The text reports modified retained residential real estate loans with concessions to financially distressed borrowers: $13.3 billion in 2021 versus $15.4 billion in 2020, including $3.9 billion and $3.9 billion of nonaccrual loans; some nonaccrual TDRs were under 90 days past due. It explains exclusions and refers to Note 12. The auto and other portfolio, mainly prime scored auto, business banking and overdrafts, declined overall as PPP forgiveness reduced business loans while auto originations supported growth; net charge-offs fell, and auto charge-off rates were 0.04% versus 0.25%. Consumer nonperforming assets fell to $5.5 billion from $6.6 billion, with residential and auto nonaccrual loans and acquired assets detailed. Notes explain exclusions for government-insured mortgages and REO, COVID deferrals, and SBA-guaranteed PPP loans.

nodes.title: Nonperforming assets
nodes.summary: The text reports modified retained residential real estate loans granted concessions to borrowers in financial difficulty, excluding insignificant or short-term changes and loans exempted from TDR accounting under the CARES Act. At year-end 2021 versus 2020, retained loans were $13.251 billion versus $15.406 billion, and nonaccrual retained loans were $3.938 billion versus $3.899 billion; some nonaccrual TDR borrowers were under 90 days past due. The auto and other portfolio, mainly prime scored auto and business banking loans and overdrafts, declined overall as business banking loans fell (largely PPP forgiveness) while scored auto lending grew. Net charge-offs fell, with scored auto charge-off rates of 0.04% in 2021 versus 0.25% in 2020. Consumer nonperforming assets totaled $5.484 billion in 2021 versus $6.619 billion in 2020, comprising nonaccrual loans and assets acquired in loan satisfactions. Notes explain exclusions for government-insured mortgages and REO, COVID-19 deferrals, and SBA-guaranteed PPP loans.

nodes.title: Nonaccrual loans
nodes.summary: The table reports changes in consumer nonaccrual loans, excluding credit cards, for 2021 and 2020. Balances moved from $6.467 billion to $5.350 billion in 2021, with $2.956 billion in additions and $4.073 billion in reductions; in 2020, they rose from $3.366 billion to $6.467 billion, with $5.892 billion in additions and $2.791 billion in reductions. Activity includes CECL-adoption PCD loans, other additions, principal payments and other reductions (including loan sales), charge-offs, returns to performing status, and foreclosures/liquidations. The 2020 additions included loans exiting COVID-19 deferral programs that were at least 90 days past due, predominantly collateral-dependent. Note 12 provides further portfolio credit-quality, delinquency, modification, and foreclosure information.

nodes.title: Purchased credit deteriorated (“PCD”) loans
nodes.summary: Reports residential real estate purchased credit-deteriorated (PCD) loan delinquency, nonaccrual, and net charge-off information for 2021 and 2020. Total PCD loans were $13.741 billion and $17.041 billion, respectively; loans 30 or more days past due were 7.24% and 5.90%. Nonaccrual loans were $1.616 billion and $1.609 billion. Net charge-offs were $15 million and $74 million, with rates of 0.10% and 0.39%. Performing loans in active COVID-19 deferral generally were not considered delinquent; nonaccrual figures include certain loans exiting deferral that were at least 90 days past due, predominantly collateral-dependent.

Consumer loans excluding credit cards increased from year-end 2020 as residential real estate growth outweighed declines in auto and other lending. The section describes portfolio composition, HELOC and interest-only mortgage terms, government-guaranteed loans, geographic concentrations, estimated loan-to-value trends, credit quality, delinquencies and risk management. It reports modified residential loans, nonaccrual balances and activity, nonperforming assets, auto charge-offs, and residential PCD loan delinquencies, nonaccruals and losses, with explanations of COVID-19 deferrals, PPP-related changes, accounting exclusions and related Note 12 disclosures.

nodes.title: Credit Card
key_items: Geographic and FICO composition of credit card loans
nodes.summary: Credit card loans grew in 2021 on strong sales, while delinquency rates and net charge-offs fell, supported by elevated consumer cash and government assistance; accrued interest and fees are covered by the allowance. The text reports geographic concentration in five states and lower balances of modified TDR loans. It describes wholesale credit risks, portfolio management and improving conditions, then presents exposure and nonperforming amounts by asset type, year-over-year changes in retained loans, commitments, criticized and nonperforming exposures, and notes on credit-risk measures, derivatives, collateral, prior-period revisions, and COVID-modified loans.

Covers JPMorgan Chase’s retained consumer portfolio, including balances, commitments, total and protected exposures, maturities, interest rates, nonaccruals, charge-offs, and calculation and scope notes. Describes COVID-19 payment deferrals, borrower outcomes, allowance treatment, and TDRs. Reviews non-card lending composition, terms, guarantees, concentrations, loan-to-value and credit-quality trends, delinquencies, modifications, nonperforming assets, and losses. Also covers credit-card growth, performance, concentrations, TDRs, risk management, exposures, criticized and nonperforming loans, and related credit-risk measures and disclosures.

nodes.title: Wholesale Credit Portfolio
Wholesale credit portfolio
nodes.summary: The text describes wholesale credit-risk sources, portfolio retention and syndication, active credit-quality and concentration monitoring, and improving 2021 conditions. It reports year-end changes in retained loans, commitments, investment-grade share, criticized exposure, and nonperforming exposure, with key drivers. A table details 2021 and 2020 credit exposures and nonperforming amounts across loans, derivatives, customer receivables, assets acquired in loan satisfactions, and commitments, plus portfolio-management credit protection and collateral. Notes define customer receivables and credit derivatives, explain revised prior figures, and state that nearly all COVID-modified loans remained performing.

nodes.title: Wholesale assistance
nodes.summary: The text describes COVID-19 assistance to wholesale clients, including payment deferrals and covenant modifications, declining retained loans in deferral from $16.8 billion in June 2020 to $107 million at year-end 2021; exited clients were largely current or repaid, and assisted loans remained monitored, risk-rated, and mostly performing. Such aid generally was not treated as TDRs under applicable relief rules, which expired January 1, 2022. Tables compare 2021 and 2020 wholesale exposure by contractual maturity and internal investment-grade ratings, including loans, derivatives net of collateral, commitments, other receivables, and credit protection. Notes explain rating criteria, loan categories, credit-derivative treatment, prior-period revisions, and maturity assumptions.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industry exposures
nodes.summary: The Firm manages and diversifies wholesale credit exposures, with added focus on industries facing actual or potential credit concerns. Criticized exposures follow U.S. banking regulatory categories (special mention, substandard, and doubtful). Excluding loans held for sale and at fair value, they fell from $41.6 billion (4.0% of wholesale exposure) in 2020 to $38.2 billion (3.5%) in 2021, due to portfolio activity and upgrades—especially in Oil & Gas and Automotive—partly offset by downgrades. Most 2021 criticized exposure was undrawn, and $35.0 billion was performing. The accompanying table presents exposures by industry for both years; industry classification generally reflects the client’s primary business, with further details in Note 4.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industries (a)
nodes.summary: The passage presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 and 2020 wholesale credit exposures by industry, including investment-grade and noninvestment-grade credit, criticized performing and nonperforming exposures, past-due loans, collateral, credit hedges, and charge-offs or recoveries. Notes define industry categories and exposure measures, explain exclusions and revised prior-period figures, and disclose additional state and municipal securities and cash placements. Real estate detail compares 2021 with 2020 by property type, listing loans and commitments, derivative receivables, credit exposure, investment-grade share, and drawn percentage; it highlights multifamily lending, criticized-exposure growth, geographic concentration, and secured versus unsecured exposure.

nodes.title: Real Estate
nodes.summary: The discussion compares JPMorgan Chase’s real estate, consumer and retail, and oil and gas credit exposures at December 31, 2021 and 2020, breaking each down by industry category into loans and lending-related commitments, derivative receivables, total credit exposure, investment-grade share, and drawn percentage. It reports total exposure and changes in criticized exposure, explaining the main drivers. Notes describe category definitions, geographic concentration, secured versus unsecured exposure, and collateral characteristics, including multifamily’s California concentration and secured portions of leisure, consumer, and oil and gas portfolios.

nodes.title: Consumer & Retail
nodes.summary: The text reports December 31, 2021 credit exposures and portfolio metrics for Consumer & Retail and Oil & Gas, with 2020 comparisons. Consumer & Retail exposure was $122.8 billion, mainly Retail, Business and Consumer Services, and Food and Beverage; criticized exposure rose $617 million to $9.9 billion due to client downgrades and portfolio activity, partly offset by upgrades. Oil & Gas exposure was $42.6 billion, including $23.1 billion in E&P and Oil Field Services; derivative receivables rose with market prices, while criticized exposure fell $4.0 billion to $1.7 billion through portfolio activity and upgrades, partly offset by downgrades. Tables provide loans and commitments, derivatives, total exposure, investment-grade percentages, and drawn ratios by subsector and year. Notes define subsectors and explain secured exposure: about 80% of Consumer & Retail non-investment-grade exposure is secured; 81% of Leisure non-investment-grade exposure is secured. Oil & Gas secured exposure was $18.0 billion in 2021 versus $13.2 billion in 2020, over half reserve-based E&P lending; unsecured exposure is largely investment-grade.

nodes.title: Oil & Gas
nodes.summary: Consumer & Retail exposure totaled $122.8 billion at year-end 2021, mainly across Retail, Business and Consumer Services, Food and Beverage, Consumer Hard Goods, and Leisure; criticized exposure rose $617 million to $9.9 billion. Oil & Gas exposure was $42.6 billion, including $23.1 billion in E&P and oilfield services; derivative receivables rose with market prices, while criticized exposure fell $4.0 billion to $1.7 billion. Tables compare 2021 and 2020 exposures, investment-grade shares, drawn percentages, and secured lending; footnotes define segments and collateral. The text also describes wholesale lending and nonaccrual loans: balances fell $1.7 billion to $2.445 billion in 2021, with activity details shown. Net charge-offs were $142 million versus $799 million in 2020, and the rate declined to 0.03% from 0.16%.

nodes.title: Loans and Wholesale Nonaccrual Activity
nodes.summary: The Firm’s wholesale businesses lend to corporate, institutional, and high-net-worth clients; Note 12 discusses delinquencies, modifications, and other credit indicators. The page reports 2021 and 2020 wholesale nonaccrual loan activity, including balances, additions, reductions, and net changes. Exposure fell $1.7 billion in 2021, mainly in Oil & Gas and Individuals and Individual Entities, as net activity and client upgrades were partly offset by downgrades. It also introduces net charge-offs/recoveries, excluding gains or losses on nonaccrual loan sales.

nodes.title: Wholesale net charge-offs/(recoveries)
nodes.summary: Wholesale loan charge-off and recovery data for 2021 and 2020: average loans retained were $526,557 million and $509,907 million, respectively; gross charge-offs were $283 million and $954 million; gross recoveries were $141 million and $155 million; net charge-offs were $142 million and $799 million; and net charge-off rates were 0.03% and 0.16%.

nodes.title: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
nodes.summary: Presents 2021 wholesale loan maturities and fixed/variable-rate distributions by loan class, plus 2020–2021 average retained loans, net charge-offs or recoveries, and rates. Explains risks and management of lending commitments and customer margin receivables. Describes derivative uses, counterparty risks, netting and collateral practices, collateral coverage, and the decline in derivative receivables from 2020 to 2021; provides net receivables after cash collateral, liquid securities, and other collateral.

nodes.title: Lending Commitments, Customer Receivables and Derivatives
nodes.summary: The page explains that lending commitments and guarantees pose maximum contractual credit risk but are often unused, so their totals do not indicate expected exposure or funding needs. Customer margin loans are collateralized, generally have no credit-loss allowance, and are managed through margin requirements and monitoring. Derivatives serve client risk-management needs and the Firm’s own risk management; credit exposure depends on counterparties and clearing, and is mitigated with netting and collateral. It reports 88% collateral coverage for relevant OTC trades in 2021 and 2020, derivative receivables of $57.1 billion and $75.4 billion, explains the decrease and collateral treatment, and introduces tables of net receivables and internal ratings.

nodes.title: Derivative receivables
nodes.summary: A table reports derivative receivables at December 31, 2021 and 2020 (in millions): total net of cash collateral was $57,081 and $75,444; after liquid securities and other cash collateral, $46,979 and $60,638; after other collateral, $45,435 and $58,802. Prior-period amounts were revised to conform with the current presentation.

nodes.title: Ratings profile of derivative receivables
nodes.summary: Derivative receivables net of collateral totaled $45.4 billion in 2021 (67% investment-grade, 33% noninvestment-grade), down from $58.8 billion in 2020 (63% and 37%). Net fair value is only a current view, so the Firm also calculates client-level Peak, DRE and AVG exposure measures, all reflecting netting and collateral. Peak is a conservative, roughly 97.5%-confidence measure used for limits and management; DRE is a less extreme, loan-equivalent measure used to aggregate credit risk; AVG estimates expected future exposure and supports pricing, capital and CVA. CVA reflects counterparty credit quality and may be adjusted for wrong-way risk. The Firm actively manages derivatives credit risk and hedges CVA changes with credit and other derivatives. Exposure profiles over ten years generally decline after year one if no new trades are added.

nodes.title: Exposure profile of derivatives measures
nodes.summary: The Firm uses credit derivatives as a market-maker and to manage its own credit risk. Credit portfolio management derivatives mitigate risks from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale derivatives counterparty exposures; other derivatives address risks such as securities held for market-making and are excluded from this category. Net protection used for portfolio management totaled $20.190 billion in 2021, down from $23.218 billion in 2020. These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting and are marked to fair value through principal transactions revenue, unlike accrual-accounted loans, creating earnings volatility that may not reflect overall credit exposure changes. CDS hedge effectiveness can vary with reference entities, contract terms, and maturity; the Firm generally aligns protection maturity with exposures and monitors and manages differences.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
nodes.summary:
Management’s discussion and analysis
Credit derivatives
The Firm uses credit derivatives for two primary purposes: first, in its capacity as a market-maker, and second, as an end-user, to manage the Firm’s own credit risk associated with various exposures.

nodes.title: Credit portfolio management activities
nodes.summary: The Firm uses credit derivatives to mitigate credit risk from lending commitments and wholesale derivatives counterparty exposures; other end-user credit derivatives, including those hedging market-making securities, are excluded. Net protection in credit portfolio management totaled $20.190 billion in 2021, down from $23.218 billion in 2020, covering loans and lending commitments and derivative receivables. These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting: fair-value gains and losses enter principal transactions revenue, while managed loans are accrual-accounted, creating earnings volatility that may not reflect overall exposure value. CDS hedge effectiveness can differ due to reference entities, contract terms, and maturities; the Firm generally aligns protection maturities with exposures and monitors and manages differences.

Describes wholesale credit-risk management, including portfolio retention and syndication, monitoring, COVID assistance, internal ratings, industry exposures, criticized and nonperforming loans, and real estate, Consumer & Retail, and Oil & Gas portfolios. Tables compare exposures, maturities, collateral, investment-grade shares, and drawn percentages across 2020–2021, with notes on classifications and methods. The section also covers nonaccrual activity, charge-offs, lending commitments, customer receivables, derivatives and collateral, derivative exposure measures and ratings, and credit-derivative hedging, protection levels, and accounting-related earnings volatility.

nodes.title: Allowance for Credit Losses
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
Allocation of allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The text explains the allowance for credit losses (ACL), its three components and balance-sheet presentation, and its decline from $30.8 billion in 2020 to $18.7 billion in 2021, driven by improved economic conditions, lower consumer and wholesale reserves, revised scenario weightings, and reduced—but continued—management adjustments for pandemic-related model distortions. It gives COVID, growth, unemployment, and supply-chain uncertainties; central-case U.S. unemployment and GDP forecasts for 2021 and 2020, notes on their definitions and future estimate updates, and references to related disclosures. Detailed tables report 2020–2021 allowance rollforwards, charge-offs, recoveries, provisions, methodologies, portfolio balances and credit ratios, plus loan-class allowance allocations and shares of retained loans; footnotes explain CECL adoption, asset-specific impairment, and credit-card nonaccrual policy.

nodes.title: Investment Portfolio Risk Management
nodes.summary: Defines investment portfolio risk as potential principal loss or reduced returns. Describes high-quality Treasury/CIO securities, their $670.1 billion 2021 carrying value and AA+ average rating, related credit, market and liquidity risks, and governance through risk committees, independent controls and approved limits. Covers principal investments, their purposes, management, COVID-19 impact, carrying values rising from $26.2 billion in 2020 to $30.5 billion in 2021, governance, stress testing and portfolio limits. Explains market-risk oversight, metrics (VaR, stress tests, drawdowns, earnings-at-risk and sensitivities), limit setting and breach escalation, pandemic monitoring, model limitations and periodic measure reviews.

Defines credit, investment and portfolio risks, exposures, governance, measurement, allowances, capital, stress testing, monitoring and reporting. Covers consumer and wholesale portfolios, including balances, commitments, maturities, ratings, concentrations, delinquencies, nonaccruals, charge-offs, modifications, collateral, hedging, derivatives, COVID-19 assistance and PPP loans. Details ACL components, trends, forecasts, methodologies and rollforwards. Also describes Treasury/CIO securities and principal investments, their risks, values, controls, market-risk metrics, limits and breach escalation.

nodes.title: Market Risk Management
Market Risk Management and Measurement
key_items: Measures used to capture market risk
nodes.summary: Market risk arises when market factors—including interest and foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities—change the value of assets and liabilities. Market Risk Management sets policies and procedures, manages risk and risk-return decisions, limits performance volatility, and reports the Firm’s risk profile. Its duties include maintaining the policy framework, independently measuring and controlling risk across business lines and the Firm, setting and monitoring limits, and conducting stress tests and qualitative assessments. Because no single metric captures market risk, it uses VaR, stress testing, profit-and-loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity measures.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and control
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase manages market risk through limits at firm, business-line, Corporate and legal-entity levels, using VaR, stress and other measures. Limits are reviewed, approved, monitored and escalated; breaches prompt corrective action or temporary increases. The text notes COVID-19 monitoring, model limitations and periodic measure enhancements. A table outlines each business’s activities, market risks, positions covered by VaR, earnings-at-risk and other sensitivity measures. VaR methodology, applications, assumptions, data and proxy limitations, model updates, and differences between one-day, 95%-confidence Risk Management VaR and ten-day, 99%-confidence Regulatory VaR are described.

nodes.title: VaR
Value-at-risk
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its historical-simulation VaR framework, based on the prior 12 months, for daily risk management and regulatory measurement. Risk Management VaR uses a one-day horizon and approximately 95% expected-tail-loss confidence level to aggregate risks, assess diversification, monitor limits, and report to management, directors, and regulators. Granular daily portfolio models are aggregated firmwide. VaR’s historical-data, liquidity, horizon, proxy, and sudden-market-change limitations are mitigated with stress testing and other measures; VaR data may differ from monthly valuation data, and models are periodically reviewed and updated. Regulatory VaR separately supports Basel III capital requirements, using covered positions, a ten-day horizon, approximately 99% confidence, and different diversification and position rules. Tables report 2021 and 2020 average, minimum, and maximum VaR by business and risk type, with notes explaining diversification, a 2020 private-equity driver, and non-comparable extrema. A July 2020 scope change excluded certain real-estate loans, with figures showing the VaR increase that would otherwise have resulted. Average VaR fell $40 million in 2021 as pandemic-era volatility rolled out of the look-back period; maximums remained elevated early in the year, while daily VaR returned toward pre-pandemic levels, as shown in a quarterly graph.

nodes.title: Total VaR
nodes.summary: The text reports the Firm’s 95%-confidence Risk Management VaR, including 2021 and 2020 averages, minima, and maxima for CIB trading risk types, credit portfolio, CCB, Corporate and other LOBs, and aggregate portfolios. It explains diversification benefits and their limitations, notes a private-equity driver of 2020 Corporate VaR, and describes a July 2020 scope change excluding certain real-estate-related loans, with the resulting adjustments to reported averages. As pandemic volatility rolled out of the one-year look-back, average Total VaR fell $40 million in 2021; maximum VaR remained elevated early in the year, while daily VaR returned to pre-pandemic levels.

nodes.title: Daily Risk Management VaR
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s daily Risk Management VaR backtesting: it compares VaR with defined daily gains and losses that exclude certain revenue components and align with Basel III requirements. An exception occurs when a loss exceeds the prior day’s VaR; the model expects about five exceptions per 100 trading days, though volatility differences can change observed counts. In 2021, the Firm had gains on 145 of 260 days and 20 exceptions, including 12 in Q4 amid unusually high interest-rate volatility. Firmwide loss days may differ from CIB Markets losses because positions and included revenue differ. A chart distributes trailing-year and fourth-quarter losses as percentages of VaR, grouping counts in 50-point intervals and showing exceptions above 100%; results differ from Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory VaR backtesting.

nodes.title: Distribution of Daily Backtesting Gains and Losses
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan’s stress-testing framework as a complement to VaR, assessing potential losses from simultaneous hypothetical market changes across rallies, sell-offs, asset classes, and geographies, including tail events, idiosyncratic risks, and basis risk. Results identify exposures, are measured against limits, and inform CCAR and other tests, risk appetite, and periodic reporting to senior management, the Board, and Board Risk Committee. Market Risk Management oversees the framework; a firmwide committee approves methodology and scenario changes, with significant changes escalated. Models follow model-risk policy. Profit-and-loss drawdowns flag trading losses above tolerance, defined as revenue falling from its year-to-date peak.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s historical-simulation Risk Management and Basel III Regulatory VaR frameworks, their horizons, confidence levels, uses, limitations, mitigations, and periodic model reviews. Reports 2020–2021 VaR by business and risk type, diversification and scope-change notes, and pandemic-related trends. Explains daily VaR backtesting, expected and observed exceptions, 2021 results, and loss distributions. Covers complementary stress testing of hypothetical market and tail events, limits, governance, reporting, model oversight, and profit-and-loss drawdown triggers.

nodes.title: Earnings-at-risk
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s structural interest rate risk, its governance, oversight, and management through securities, derivatives, and firmwide transfer pricing. It describes factors driving risk and earnings-at-risk simulations, including rate scenarios, balance-sheet and prepayment assumptions, and deposit pricing; notes the measure is not an income forecast; and reports 2021 versus 2020 sensitivities. U.S. dollar sensitivities declined across parallel, steepening, and flattening scenarios, mainly reflecting baseline and balance-sheet changes and assets repricing faster than deposits. Non-U.S. dollar sensitivities were broadly stable, with steepening scenarios immaterial.

nodes.title: Non-U.S. Dollar FX Risk
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. dollar FX risk arises when exchange-rate changes affect the Firm’s assets, liabilities, or future results. Structural exposures stem from capital investments, forecasted expenses and revenue, investment securities, and foreign-currency debt. Treasury and CIO, in partnership with the LOBs, primarily manage these risks and may hedge some exposures with derivatives.

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.summary: The text reports sensitivity-based market-risk measures for debt, equity and funding activities excluded from VaR or earnings-at-risk, explaining that results may not predict realized outcomes and that hedges are generally netted. It lists 2021 and 2020 impacts, scenarios, recognition channels (net revenue, OCI or noninterest expense), and related scope and methodology notes. It then describes country risk exposure, independent oversight and responsibilities, exposure attribution and limitations, measurement rules for lending, deposits, securities financing, securities, derivatives and credit protection, and differences from FFIEC reporting.

Explains market-risk sources, governance, measurement, monitoring and control across the Firm, including policies, limits, escalation, stress tests and multiple complementary measures. Covers VaR frameworks, methodology, limitations, business-level results, backtesting and stress testing; structural interest-rate risk and earnings-at-risk assumptions and sensitivities; non-U.S.-dollar FX exposures and hedging; and other sensitivity-based measures for activities outside VaR or earnings-at-risk. Also describes country-risk oversight, exposure measurement, reporting differences and limitations.

nodes.title: Country Risk Management
nodes.summary: Describes country risk management: its independent governance and responsibilities, exposure attribution and measurement across lending, deposits, securities, derivatives and other activities, differences from FFIEC reporting, stress testing, COVID-19 monitoring, regular limit and exposure reporting, and the top 20 non-U.S. country exposures for 2021 versus 2020, including key changes and table definitions. It then outlines operational risk and the CCOR framework, governance and business responsibilities, risk identification and control assessments, quantitative measurement and capital modeling (including LDA, AMA and stress testing), and independent monitoring and testing.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Management
Operational Risk Management Framework
key_items: Operational Risk Governance; Operational Risk Identification; Operational Risk Measurement
Management of Operational Risk; Operational Risk Reporting
nodes.summary: Operational risk arises from failed processes or systems, human factors, or external events, and includes compliance, conduct, legal, and model risk. The Firm’s CCOR framework governs, identifies, measures, monitors, tests, manages, and reports these risks. LOBs and Corporate manage risk and controls; central leadership sets standards, oversees assessments, and reports to the Board. Risk identification uses self-assessments and independent challenge. Measurement combines control reviews, historical-loss modeling, capital estimates, scenarios, and stress testing. Monitoring tests compliance and controls; issues are escalated and remediated through action plans. Firmwide reporting tracks indicators and risk appetite, with escalation to senior management and the Board.

nodes.title: Subcategories and examples of operational risks
key_items: Business and technology resiliency risk; Payment fraud risk; Third-party outsourcing risk
nodes.summary: The text outlines operational-risk categories—compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risk—and examples including cybersecurity, business and technology resiliency, payment fraud, and third-party outsourcing. It describes cyber threats from malicious actors, business growth, vendors, and clients; investments and controls to prevent, detect, and respond to incidents; governance, oversight, response planning, resilience measures, and mandatory employee security and privacy training. It also covers disruption preparedness, payment-fraud controls and education, and frameworks for selecting, monitoring, and managing suppliers and affiliates.

nodes.title: Insurance
nodes.summary:
Insurance
One of the ways in which operational risk may be mitigated is through insurance maintained by the Firm. The Firm purchases insurance from commercial insurers and maintains a wholly-owned captive insurer, Park Assurance Company. Insurance may also be required by third parties with whom the Firm does business.

nodes.title: Compliance Risk Management
nodes.summary: Compliance risk is the risk of violating laws, regulations, rules, or conduct standards. Business lines and Corporate own and manage this risk, while the independent Operational Risk and Compliance organization oversees, monitors, tests, and reports on it through policies and standards. Risks span products, client relationships, employee conduct, anti-money laundering, trading, market conduct, cross-border activity, and fiduciary duties. Governance is led by the Global CCO and designated risk executive under the CCOR framework, with updates to Board committees and possible special committees for Consent Orders. The Code of Conduct sets integrity expectations, requires reporting violations and annual employee affirmation, and provides ongoing training and an anonymous, globally available hotline (subject to local laws); retaliation for good-faith reporting is prohibited, and the Audit Committee periodically receives program reports.

nodes.title: Conduct Risk Management
nodes.summary: Conduct risk is operational risk arising from employee actions or inaction that may harm customers, market integrity, or the Firm’s reputation. Each line of business and Corporate is responsible for managing it in line with the Firm’s business principles and Code, which guide ethical, lawful conduct. The CCOR Management policy governs the program’s risk management framework. A senior forum sets strategic direction, connects initiatives, and reviews the Firmwide risk appetite assessment. Management covers the employee life cycle, while business units and designated functions periodically assess risk, review relevant metrics and issues, and provide education.

nodes.title: Legal Risk Management
nodes.summary: Legal risk is operational risk arising from actual or alleged failure to meet legal obligations under applicable law, client agreements, and the Firm’s products and services. The global Legal function manages litigation, enforcement, reviews and investigations; advises on products, contracts, disclosures, marketing, new initiatives, laws, regulatory changes, advocacy, and business units and leadership; resolves disputes; manages outside counsel; and advises the Conflicts Office on potentially conflicted wholesale transactions. The General Counsel reports to the CEO and serves on key risk and control committees. Legal reports significant matters to the Board and Audit Committee, advises committees and business units, and addresses potential reputation risks.

nodes.title: Estimations and Model Risk Management
nodes.summary: Estimation and model risk is the operational risk of adverse decisions caused by incorrect or misused outputs. JPMorgan uses models and other analytical or judgment-based estimates for valuation, risk measurement, regulatory capital, stress testing, credit-loss allowances and business decisions. Independent Model Risk Governance and Review (MRGR) sets relevant policies and governs these estimates. Model users and developers own model risks and are responsible for development, implementation, testing, MRGR referral, ongoing monitoring and maintenance, and appropriate enhancements. Models are tiered by complexity, exposure and reliance; MRGR approves tiers and reviews suitability, methodology and assumptions, requiring additional tests such as back-testing as needed. MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before use, though exceptions may allow interim use with risk mitigations. Model uncertainty can increase when markets differ from training conditions, as during early COVID-19, requiring greater judgment and analytical adjustments. The text refers readers to critical accounting estimates and Note 2 for valuation methods.

The section describes the Firm’s operational risk framework: how business units and central functions identify, assess, measure, monitor, test, remediate, escalate, and report risks under CCOR, including compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risk. It covers examples such as cybersecurity, resilience, payment fraud, and third-party risks, related controls and employee training, and insurance mitigation. It explains governance and responsibilities for compliance, ethical conduct and reporting, legal advice and disputes, and model development, independent review, approval, monitoring, and uncertainty.

Covers JPMorgan Chase’s firmwide risk framework, risk appetite, three lines of defense, and Board, management, and independent risk governance, including committee oversight and escalation. Describes strategic, capital, liquidity, reputation, credit and investment, market, country, and operational risks: their identification, measurement, controls, stress testing, monitoring, reporting, and mitigation. Topics include strategic planning and capital allocation; liquidity and reputation policies; consumer and wholesale credit exposures, allowances, and portfolio trends; Treasury and investment risks; market-risk metrics, interest rates, and foreign exchange; country exposures; and operational, compliance, conduct, legal, and model risks, including cybersecurity, resilience, fraud, third parties, training, insurance, and model governance.

nodes.title: Critical Accounting Estimates Used by the Firm
Allowance for credit losses
key_items: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its controlled, consistently applied accounting estimates and management judgment. Its $18.7 billion credit-loss allowance covers amortized-cost assets and certain lending commitments, with judgments involving forecasts, historical losses, risk ratings, collateral and expected life. Estimates use five weighted macroeconomic scenarios and hundreds of variables; scenario weights shifted toward a more balanced outlook in 2021, while pandemic-related modeling adjustments continued. A central-versus-adverse sensitivity analysis showed modeled increases of about $550 million for residential real estate, $2.6 billion for credit cards and $3.0 billion for wholesale exposures, but is not a forecast of total allowance changes. The Firm considers its estimates reasonable despite uncertainty.

nodes.title: Fair value
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase reports recurring and nonrecurring fair-value assets and liabilities, including 2021 asset totals and Level 3 proportions, with a note on derivative netting. Fair-value estimates depend on observable inputs, models, management judgment, and adjustments for credit, funding, liquidity, and market risk; uncertainty can affect reported gains or losses. Goodwill is tested annually, and no impairment was identified in 2021, with reporting-unit fair values exceeding carrying values by at least 10%. The credit-card rewards liability rose to $9.8 billion, driven mainly by earnings outpacing redemptions, and is sensitive to redemption and cost assumptions. Income-tax accounting requires judgment amid complex, differing laws and potential disputes with tax authorities.

nodes.title: Valuation, Goodwill Impairment and Rewards Liability
nodes.summary: The text explains management judgment and uncertainty in valuing Level 2 and 3 instruments, including adjustments, assumptions, and the potential effects of alternative methods. Goodwill is allocated to reporting units and tested annually; in 2021, economic conditions and projections were assessed, and no impairment was found, with fair values at least 10% above carrying values. It also describes credit-card rewards, liability accounting and balances ($9.8 billion in 2021 versus $7.7 billion in 2020), drivers of the increase, sensitivity to redemption-rate and cost-per-point assumptions, and the estimated $265 million liability increase under specified assumption changes.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase explains that complex, varying tax laws require judgments about tax interpretations, timing, uncertain positions and potential disputes, which may be resolved through audits, appeals or courts and could materially affect results or the effective tax rate. It reviews and updates tax estimates and unrecognized benefits as laws, guidance and circumstances change. Deferred taxes reflect book-tax differences and enacted rates; deferred tax assets, including NOL and foreign tax credit carryforwards, are assessed for realizability using future-income estimates and tax strategies, with valuation allowances established or reversed as appropriate. Management concluded assets were realizable, net of allowances, at December 31, 2021. Current and deferred provisions are estimates; differences identified when returns are filed generally affect taxes in that period. Further detail is in Note 25.

nodes.title: Accounting and Reporting Developments
nodes.summary: The text describes FASB reference rate reform guidance, issued in March 2020 and updated in January 2021. It offers optional expedients and elections for contract amendments, hedge accounting, and related transactions, including treating certain amendments and discounting-transition derivative changes as modifications, preserving hedge relationships, and transferring eligible securities from held-to-maturity classification. The guidance became effective upon issuance. JPMorgan Chase adopted certain contract-modification and hedge-accounting expedients in Q3 2020 and applied the discounting-transition election retrospectively; these choices eased administrative burdens and had no material financial statement impact.

nodes.title: Forward-Looking Statements
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s forward-looking statements describe expectations, may appear in filings or oral communications, are subject to risks, may differ materially from actual results, and are not updated except through later disclosures. Listed risks include pandemic and geopolitical/economic conditions; laws, regulation, policy, inflation and taxes; markets, credit, capital and liquidity; reputation, social and environmental concerns; technology, controls, products, competition, employees and expenses; litigation, accounting, valuation, disasters, operational resilience and cyber threats, plus risks in the 2021 Form 10-K. Management’s report explains internal-control responsibilities, purpose, scope and inherent limits; reports an effective assessment under COSO 2013 with no material weaknesses as of December 31, 2021; and notes PwC’s audit. It is signed by James Dimon and Jeremy Barnum, dated February 22, 2022.

summary: Reviews JPMorgan Chase’s business, 2021 results, financial condition, cash flows, segment performance, and non-GAAP measures, alongside COVID-19 and benchmark-rate transition developments. Describes firmwide governance and risk management, key accounting estimates, and accounting changes. It also discusses forward-looking-statement risks and management’s internal-control assessment, which found controls effective with no material weaknesses, as reported to the auditors.

nodes.title: Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase management is responsible for designing and maintaining internal control over financial reporting to provide reasonable assurance of reliable U.S. GAAP reporting, accurate records, authorized transactions, and protection against material asset misuse. Controls have inherent limitations and may weaken or become inadequate over time. Using the COSO 2013 framework, management assessed controls as effective, with no material weaknesses, as of December 31, 2021. PwC independently audited their effectiveness. The report is signed by CEO James Dimon and CFO Jeremy Barnum and dated February 22, 2022.

Fair Value of Certain Level 3 Financial Instruments

It notes a 2020 change in credit-loss accounting and describes management and auditor responsibilities, PCAOB audit procedures, and internal-control definitions and limitations. Critical audit matters cover loan-loss allowances—especially economic forecasts, models, and adjustments—and Level 3 fair values, with procedures for testing controls, assumptions, data, and estimates. nodes.title: Consolidated statements of income

The income statement covers revenue components, interest income and expense, net revenue, credit-loss provisions, expense categories, pretax income, taxes, net income and common earnings, earnings per share, and weighted-average shares. nodes.title: Consolidated statements of comprehensive income

nodes.title: Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 and 2020 consolidated balance sheets list assets, liabilities, and stockholders’ equity, with fair-value, pledged-asset, and allowance details. nodes.title: Consolidated statements of cash flows

A footnote notes revised prior-period operating amounts; the financial statement notes are integral to the statement.

nodes.title: Offsetting assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP allows net presentation of certain derivatives, related collateral, and securities financing balances when specified conditions—including an enforceable master netting agreement—are met; the Firm nets eligible balances. These agreements mitigate counterparty credit risk by enabling covered transactions to be terminated, valued, and settled as one net payment after default. Related collateral or margin agreements require net deficit coverage (subject to thresholds) and allow the demanding party to offset amounts owed against collateral or liquidate it upon default. See Notes 5 and 11 for details on derivatives and securities financing agreements.

nodes.title: Statements of cash flows

nodes.title: Accounting standard adopted January 1, 2020
nodes.summary: Effective January 1, 2020, the Firm adopted CECL, creating a unified allowance framework for amortized-cost financial assets and certain off-balance-sheet credit exposures. The framework estimates credit losses over each instrument’s remaining expected life and incorporates anticipated macroeconomic changes, replacing the prior estimate of probable losses inherent in retained loan portfolios and certain lending commitments. Adoption reduced retained earnings by $2.7 billion.

nodes.title: Significant accounting policies
nodes.summary: Lists JPMorgan Chase’s significant accounting policies and directs readers to the notes and pages containing detailed descriptions: fair value measurement and option; derivatives; revenue and expenses; interest; employee benefits and incentives; investments and securities financing; loans and credit-loss allowance; variable interest entities; goodwill and mortgage servicing rights; premises, equipment and leases; long-term debt; earnings per share; taxes; off-balance-sheet lending, guarantees and commitments; and litigation (Notes 2–30, pages 169–290).

Explains JPMorgan Chase’s business, accounting basis under U.S. GAAP and regulatory requirements, and prior-period reclassifications. Covers consolidation of entities and investments, fiduciary-asset exclusions, VIE and SPE assessments and reassessments, revenue recognition, estimation uncertainty, foreign-currency accounting, and permitted netting of derivatives and securities-financing balances. Defines cash for cash-flow statements; summarizes the 2020 adoption of CECL and its retained-earnings impact; and lists significant accounting policies with references to detailed disclosures.

nodes.title: Note 2 - Fair value measurement
Valuation process
nodes.summary: JPMorgan measures some assets, liabilities, and lending commitments at fair value either regularly or in specified circumstances. Fair value reflects an orderly market-participant transaction, using quoted prices where available and otherwise models with observable or unobservable inputs; estimates involve judgment and may differ from other participants’ estimates. Risk-taking functions produce valuations, while the independent Valuation Control Group verifies prices and estimates, applies adjustments, and reports within governance overseen by senior finance and risk executives. Verification uses market data and additional reviews for less observable valuations, with heightened review for significant or complex positions. Adjustments may address liquidity, large net open positions, uncertainty in unobservable inputs, counterparty and own credit risk (CVA/DVA), and funding (FVA); Level 1 quoted prices are not adjusted.

nodes.title: Valuation model review and approval
nodes.summary: When market prices or comparable quotes are unavailable, fair value is estimated with models using relevant transaction terms and market-based or independently sourced inputs; those inputs undergo the described price-verification process. Under Firm policy, MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before operational use. Exceptions may permit interim use before approval, potentially subject to MRGR-required risk mitigations, such as limiting trading activity.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: The text defines the U.S. GAAP fair value hierarchy: Level 1 uses quoted prices for identical instruments in active markets, Level 2 uses other observable inputs, and Level 3 includes significant unobservable inputs; classification follows the lowest significant input level. It outlines valuation methods and hierarchy classifications for securities financing, wholesale and consumer loans, securities, commodities, derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, private equity and fund investments, VIE interests, and structured notes. Methods include quoted or comparable prices, broker quotes, discounted cash flows, models, NAV, and underlying-asset values, with relevant market, credit, collateral, prepayment, volatility, correlation, liquidity, and adjustment inputs. It also notes CVA, FVA, and DVA adjustments and introduces fair-value asset and liability tables for 2021 and 2020.

nodes.title: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s recurring fair-value assets and liabilities at December 31, 2021 and 2020, broken down by instrument and fair-value hierarchy levels 1–3, including derivative netting adjustments. Notes explain mortgage-related GSE obligations, physical-commodity valuation, offsetting long and short securities, investments using NAV, loan composition, derivative netting, and revised prior-year presentation. The text also describes level 3 valuation governance, judgment and input selection, listed techniques and significant unobservable inputs, and cautions that input ranges and averages reflect instrument characteristics rather than uncertainty or estimate reasonableness.

nodes.title: Fair value measurements using significant unobservable inputs
Level 3 valuations
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s processes and judgment for valuing Level 3 instruments, including selecting models and deriving significant unobservable inputs from empirical data. It describes how to interpret disclosed input ranges and averages, noting observable components are excluded and hedged using Level 1/2 positions. A 2021 table lists principal Level 3 instruments, fair values, valuation techniques, unobservable inputs, ranges and averages. Footnotes clarify aggregation, instrument composition, structured notes, other assets, price conventions, forward equity pricing and averaging methods.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s Level 3 recurring fair-value measurements: classification depends on significant unobservable inputs, though valuations also include observable components; related gains and losses exclude the impact of Level 1 and 2 hedges. It presents 2019–2021 rollforwards for Level 3 assets and liabilities, covering trading securities, derivatives, available-for-sale securities, loans, mortgage servicing rights, deposits, borrowings, trading liabilities, VIE interests and debt. Notes disclose Level 3 shares of fair-valued assets and liabilities, net derivative presentation, income-statement/OCI treatment, loan originations, settlement-related items and revised prior-period presentation.

It explains derivative credit valuation adjustments (CVA) and funding valuation adjustments (FVA), their methods and key inputs, and their reported revenue impacts. It also describes how own-credit-risk DVA on fair-value-option liabilities is measured and how realized and unrealized effects are reported.

Presents 2019–2021 Level 3 asset and liability rollforwards, composition, accounting treatment, and transfers between Levels 2 and 3; highlights 2021 asset changes, including MSR growth. key_items: Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.summary: Explains derivative credit and funding valuation adjustments: CVA estimates counterparty default losses using exposure scenarios, CDS-based default probabilities and recovery rates, and mitigations such as collateral and offset rights; FVA reflects market-participant funding costs, including the Firm’s credit risk for derivative liabilities, while collateralized derivatives use overnight indexed swap discounting and need no separate FVA. nodes.title: Assets and Liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis
nodes.summary: The text reports assets and liabilities subject to nonrecurring fair value adjustments at December 31, 2021 and 2020, by product category and fair value hierarchy, with totals for loans, other assets, and liabilities. nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values

The text reports 2021 and 2020 carrying values and upward/downward changes, including cumulative changes since 2018, and describes approximately 40 million Visa Class B shares held at nominal value, subject to transfer restrictions and future conversion at a potentially adjustable rate. nodes.title: Note 3 - Fair value option
Note 3 - Fair value option (intro)
nodes.summary: The fair value option allows selected financial assets, liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments and written loan commitments to be measured at fair value. The Firm elects it to reduce income-statement volatility from mismatched accounting bases and to reflect instruments managed at fair value. Elections cover certain loans and lending commitments, securities financing agreements, securitized-asset interests with embedded credit derivatives, client-driven structured notes and other hybrid instruments, and certain long-term interests issued by CIB consolidated securitization trusts whose underlying assets are at fair value.

nodes.summary: The note explains how JPMorgan Chase identifies and manages credit-risk concentrations: consumer exposures are monitored by product and U.S. region, wholesale exposures by industry and client, with senior oversight, collateral, underwriting changes, syndications, sales, securitizations, derivatives, netting and other mitigants.
