nodes.title: Note 5 - Derivative instruments
Derivative Activities, Risk Management and Clearing
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase uses derivatives primarily for client market-making and risk management, deriving value from underlying assets, rates, indices or other inputs. It offsets client exposures with other derivatives or financial instruments. Risk management derivatives address interest-rate, foreign-exchange, commodity-inventory and counterparty-credit risks, with gains or losses expected to substantially offset related variability; credit derivatives, mainly CDS, provide compensation after specified credit events. Contracts include bilateral OTC derivatives, exchange-traded futures and options, and OTC-cleared derivatives novated to CCPs. The Firm also clears client contracts as a clearing member but does not report those contracts in its consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Accounting for derivatives
Accounting for derivatives (intro)
nodes.summary: The Firm records all freestanding derivatives executed for its own account at fair value on its consolidated balance sheets. Under U.S. GAAP, derivative assets and liabilities and related cash collateral may be offset when a legally enforceable master netting agreement exists. Changes in derivative value depend on hedge-accounting designation and qualification; derivatives not designated as hedges are measured at fair value through earnings. The referenced disclosures provide details on derivative balances and gains and losses, while Notes 2 and 3 discuss embedded derivatives in structured notes.

nodes.title: Derivatives netting and collateral

nodes.title: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes derivative counterparty credit risk and mitigants, including enforceable netting and collateral agreements, and liquidity risk from collateral and termination requirements triggered by fair-value changes or credit downgrades. The text reports 2021 and 2020 net derivative payables and collateral posted, plus single- and two-notch downgrade liquidity impacts for OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives, noting rating-threshold and initial-margin qualifications and revised prior-period figures. nodes.title: Gains and losses on derivatives related to market-making activities and other derivatives

Credit derivatives transfer third-party issuer credit risk from protection buyers to sellers, who receive premiums but may owe payments after credit events; buyers face seller credit risk. The Firm buys and sells credit protection to serve customers and manages lending, counterparty, and market-making credit exposures with these instruments.

nodes.title: Credit default swaps
nodes.summary: Credit default swaps (CDS) reference a single entity, an index, or a portfolio; the Firm buys and sells protection through OTC or cleared contracts. Single-name CDS manage one entity’s default risk, while index CDS address broader markets and track portfolios that are periodically revised; defaulted entities are removed. Customized portfolio exposures, including protection for specified loss tranches, are also possible. After a credit event, the buyer claims from the seller the difference between contract face value and the reference obligation’s recovery value, without recourse to the entity or any requirement to own its debt.

nodes.title: Credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Credit-related notes are funded credit derivatives: investors pay par upfront for periodic credit-risk-based payments and repayment at maturity, except after a specified credit event, when settlement reflects the reference obligation’s recovery value; neither party has recourse to the defaulting entity. The Firm reports year-end 2021 and 2020 notional amounts of credit derivatives and notes sold and purchased. Protection sellers typically pay less than full net notional, and the Firm offsets sold protection with identical or similar protection. Other purchased protection includes related reference positions and market-making notes; notes protecting retained consumer loans are excluded from the tables. Notional amounts are not the Firm’s primary risk measure because they omit event probability, recovery value, and related instruments and hedges.

nodes.title: Pension Plan Assumptions and Investments
nodes.summary: Expected long-term returns reflect asset-weighted forward-looking estimates adjusted for market conditions and plan portfolios; benefit-obligation discount rates are generally set by actuaries, with the principal pension plan matching bond yields to projected cash flows. Plan assets are diversified across investments and regularly reviewed and rebalanced. Principal-plan allocation ranges are 42–100% debt, 0–40% equity, 0–3% real estate, and 0–12% alternatives. Pension and OPEB plans generally exclude JPMorgan securities except for indirect third-party fund exposure, while holding $2.5 billion and $2.7 billion in affiliate-sponsored or managed investments in 2021 and 2020, respectively.

nodes.title: Fair value measurement of the plans’ assets and liabilities

Pension plan assets and liabilities measured at fair value

Note 10 - Investment securities (intro)

nodes.title: Note 12 - Loans
Loan accounting framework
key_items: Interest income; Nonaccrual loans; Allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The note explains loan accounting by strategy: held-for-investment, held-for-sale, or fair value. It covers amortized-cost measurement, interest and fee recognition, accrued interest, nonaccrual and return-to-accrual rules, and the credit-loss allowance. It details consumer and wholesale charge-off triggers, collateral valuation methods and update practices. Held-for-sale loans use lower of cost or fair value, while fair-value-option loans are marked to fair value; both recognize specified income and fees differently and are excluded from allowance and charge-off policies but remain subject to nonaccrual rules.

nodes.title: Loan classification changes
nodes.summary: Loans moved from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value, with credit losses charged to the allowance and other losses recognized in noninterest revenue; loans moved back are recorded at amortized cost and assessed for impairment. Loan modifications may offer concessions such as rate reductions, extensions, deferrals, forgiveness, or asset transfers and are generally TDRs unless insignificant. TDRs are generally placed on nonaccrual (with limited exceptions), may return to accrual after at least six months or six payments and evidence of likely repayment, and generally remain subject to asset-specific impairment assessment. Most COVID-19 modifications were not TDRs due to their short-term or insignificant nature or temporary CARES Act relief; others were treated as TDRs. Eligible deferred loans were not placed on nonaccrual, expected losses were included in the allowance, and assistance could delay delinquency, nonaccrual, and charge-off recognition.

nodes.title: Foreclosed property
nodes.summary: The Firm acquires real, commercial, and personal property through loan restructurings, workouts, and foreclosures, recognizing it when received in satisfaction of a loan. Real estate is generally recognized at a foreclosure sale or upon execution of a deed in lieu. Foreclosed assets are reported in other assets at fair value less estimated selling costs, reviewed quarterly, and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value; subsequent valuation changes affect noninterest revenue, while taxes and maintenance are other expenses. Foreclosures resumed after a temporary COVID-19 suspension.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio

It presents retained, held-for-sale, and fair-value loan balances by segment for 2021 and 2020, clarifies exclusions and netting in reported balances, and summarizes retained-loan purchases, sales, and reclassifications to held-for-sale for both years.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards are primarily scored prime-market mortgages, home equity, auto, and business banking loans, also including junior-lien, interest-only, and payment-option loans that may negatively amortize. Retained loans totaled $295.6 billion at year-end 2021 ($224.8 billion residential real estate; $70.8 billion auto and other), versus $302.1 billion in 2020; PPP loans included in Business Banking were $5.4 billion and $19.2 billion, respectively. Delinquency rates indicate credit quality, with over-30-day delinquency an early warning and residential real estate delinquency over 150 days strongly signaling likely liquidation. Other indicators include residential loan LTV/combined LTV, collateral geography, and refreshed FICO scores; high LTV combined with low FICO signals greater default risk. Geography also indicates performance for scored auto and business banking loans.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.summary: The text reports retained residential mortgage delinquency by origination year and revolving-loan status for 2021 and 2020, with explanatory notes on government-insured loans, COVID-19 deferrals, purchased loans, and revised figures. It describes lien positions and higher delinquencies among revolving loans converted to term loans. It also presents nonaccrual and government-guaranteed past-due balances, estimated loan-to-value and FICO categories, weighted averages, and geographic distribution, with definitions and accounting details. nodes.title: Nature and extent of modifications
nodes.summary: The text explains that Firm and government (including U.S. GSE) modification programs offer troubled borrowers concessions such as reduced interest rates, extended terms or payments, and deferred principal or interest. A table reports residential-loan TDR trial approvals and permanent modifications for 2019–2021, plus the percentages of permanent modifications granting each concession: rate reductions, extensions, deferrals, forgiveness, or other concessions. It excludes specified Chapter 7, insignificant or short-term modifications, and loans under the CARES Act accounting suspension. Concessions commonly overlap; trial terms are generally consistent with permanent terms. “Other” includes variable-to-fixed rates and qualifying payment delays.

nodes.title: Financial effects of modifications and redefaults
nodes.summary: The table reports financial effects of permanent residential real estate loan TDR modifications and balances of loans that redefaulted within one year for 2019–2021; it excludes trial modifications, specified non-concessions and Chapter 7 cases, and loans subject to CARES Act TDR accounting suspension. It presents before-and-after weighted-average interest rates and remaining terms, modification charge-offs, principal deferred and forgiven, and redefaulted loan balances. Redefault means two payments past due; such loans are generally liquidated, and recent redefault data may not indicate ultimate levels. At year-end 2021, modified loans had an estimated four-year remaining life, including expected voluntary and forced prepayments.

nodes.title: Note 13 - Allowance for credit losses
Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lendingrelated commitments

nodes.title: Note 14 - Variable interest entities

nodes.title: Consolidated VIE assets and liabilities

nodes.title: VIEs sponsored by third parties
key_items: Tax credit vehicles; Customer municipal bond vehicles (TOB trusts)

For qualifying sales, gains or losses reflect proceeds received—including cash, beneficial interests, or servicing assets—less the assets’ carrying value and are reported as noninterest revenue.

nodes.title: Securitization activity

nodes.title: Note 20 - Long-term debt

The note presents debt carrying values by maturity and issuer for 2021 and 2020, with interest-rate and accounting details. It describes secured, fair-value and zero-coupon debt, beneficial interests, callable debt, upcoming annual maturities, and revised prior-period figures. It reports contractual and derivative-adjusted average rates, subsidiary debt guarantees, and confirms unsecured debt has no specified rating- or performance-triggered acceleration, borrowing limits or collateral requirements.

nodes.title: Note 21 - Preferred stock
nodes.summary: The note describes JPMorgan Chase’s authorized preferred stock, its seniority to common stock in liquidation, and outstanding non-cumulative fixed-rate and fixed-to-floating series at December 31, 2021 and 2020, including shares, carrying values, issue dates, rates, redemption dates, and dividends. It explains depositary shares, rate benchmarks and conversion terms, dividend timing and prorating, and series-specific rate changes. Each share has a $10,000 liquidation value and redemption price plus unpaid dividends; aggregate liquidation value was $35.2 billion in 2021. It also lists redemptions in 2020–2022 and states redemption rights, capital-treatment-event provisions, and Federal Reserve non-objection requirements.

nodes.title: Note 22 - Common stock
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase was authorized to issue 9 billion $1-par common shares in 2020 and 2021. The text reports 2019–2021 share issuance, treasury purchases and reissuances, and year-end shares outstanding, plus repurchase volumes and costs. It describes Federal Reserve limits on capital distributions during the pandemic, their expiration in June 2021, and a Board-authorized repurchase program of up to $30 billion. Repurchases are discretionary, subject to market, regulatory, capital and investment factors, have no price targets or timetable, and may use open-market, private or Rule 10b5-1 transactions. About 58.3 million shares were reserved for employee and director plans at year-end 2021.

nodes.title: Note 23 - Earnings per share
nodes.summary: Note 23 explains JPMorgan Chase’s EPS methods: basic EPS uses the two-class method, allocating earnings between common stock and participating unvested RSUs that receive nonforfeitable dividends; these RSUs are excluded from diluted incremental shares. Diluted EPS considers contingently issuable shares and reports the more dilutive result of the two-class and treasury stock methods; the two-class method was more dilutive in 2019–2021. The table reports annual net income, preferred dividends, participating-security allocations, common-stockholder income, weighted-average basic and diluted shares, dilutive awards, and basic and diluted EPS for those years.

nodes.title: Note 24 - Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.summary: Note 24 defines accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI), covering after-tax investment-security unrealized gains/losses, currency translation and hedges, fair-value and cash-flow hedges, defined-benefit pension/OPEB items, and own-credit-risk changes on fair-value-option liabilities. Tables show component balances through 2018–2021 and pre-tax, tax, and after-tax OCI changes for 2019–2021. A footnote identifies $2.4 billion of unamortized after-tax gains on AFS securities transferred to HTM; accompanying notes explain income-statement reclassifications, translation-related entity liquidations, excluded cross-currency basis spreads, and where cash-flow hedge amounts are recorded.

nodes.title: Note 25 - Income taxes
Effective tax rate and expense
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase files consolidated U.S. federal tax returns and uses the asset-liability method, recognizing current and deferred taxes and valuation allowances; tax estimates may change as jurisdictional audits are settled. In 2021, deferred investment tax credits were reclassified, increasing tax expense and other income but not net income, with prior periods revised. The note reconciles effective tax rates for 2019–2021 (18.8%, 18.7%, 18.9%) and reports current, deferred, and total tax expense by jurisdiction: $8.435 billion, $6.684 billion, and $11.228 billion, respectively. Audit resolutions produced tax expense of $69 million in 2021 and benefits of $72 million and $1.1 billion in 2020 and 2019. Equity-recorded tax effects increased by $2.0 billion in 2021 and decreased by $827 million and $862 million in 2020 and 2019.

nodes.title: Results from Non-U.S. earnings
key_items: Note 25 – Income taxes; Effective tax rate and expense; Effective tax rate
Tax effect of items recorded in stockholders’ equity
nodes.summary: The table reports income before income tax expense by U.S. and non-U.S. operations for 2021, 2020, and 2019, totaling $59.562 billion, $35.815 billion, and $44.866 billion, respectively. Non-U.S. income means income generated by operations outside the U.S.; a prior-period figure was revised to match the current presentation. Any U.S. tax on global intangible low-tax income will be recognized as income tax expense when incurred.

nodes.title: Affordable housing tax credits
nodes.summary: The Firm recognized affordable-housing investment tax credits and other tax benefits of $1.7 billion in 2021 and $1.5 billion in both 2020 and 2019; related amortization was $1.3 billion, $1.2 billion, and $1.1 billion, respectively. Investment carrying values were $10.8 billion at year-end 2021 and $9.7 billion at year-end 2020, while related commitments were $4.6 billion and $3.8 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Deferred taxes
nodes.summary: Deferred tax expense or benefit arises from differences between financial-reporting and tax-return measurements. Deferred tax assets are recognized when realization is more likely than not; otherwise, a valuation allowance is recorded. The table presents 2021 and 2020 deferred tax asset and liability categories and net balances. At year-end 2021, JPMorgan Chase had $615 million of deferred tax assets related to tax-loss and other attribute carryforwards, with specified balances and expiration periods: some U.S. and non-U.S. attributes expire from 2026–2037 and 2026–2036, respectively, while others carry forward indefinitely; FTCs expire in 2029–2030 and state/local capital losses in 2022. The valuation allowance relates to state and local capital losses, FTCs, and certain non-U.S. deferred tax assets, including NOLs.

nodes.title: Unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase reported unrecognized tax benefits of $4.6 billion, $4.3 billion and $4.0 billion at year-end 2021, 2020 and 2019; $3.4 billion, $3.1 billion and $2.8 billion, respectively, would reduce the effective tax rate if recognized. Other items would have no effective-rate impact due to temporary differences or offsetting deductions and jurisdictional benefits. Audits, particularly by the IRS, could change the gross balance by up to about $300 million over 12 months, through settlement payments or income-statement recognition. A reconciliation details annual increases and decreases, including cash settlements. After-tax interest expense and penalties were $174 million, $147 million and a $52 million benefit in 2021, 2020 and 2019; accrued interest and penalties were $1.1 billion and $1.0 billion at year-end 2021 and 2020.

nodes.title: Tax examination status
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase reports ongoing IRS and global, state, and local tax examinations, listing U.S., New York State and City, California, and U.K. periods and examination statuses. The note explains regulatory restrictions on cash and other assets: restricted cash totaled $19.7 billion in 2021 versus $24.4 billion in 2020, with additional customer-related pledged cash and securities and restricted securities disclosed. It also describes legal limits on bank-affiliate lending and covered transactions, the roles and funding relationships of the Parent Company and intermediate holding company, regulator and capital/liquidity constraints on dividends and credit, and about $20 billion of subsidiary dividend capacity without prior approval at January 1, 2022.

Covers JPMorgan Chase’s income-tax accounting, effective-rate reconciliation and current/deferred tax expense by jurisdiction for 2019–2021, audit settlements, equity-recorded tax effects, and U.S. versus non-U.S. earnings. It describes affordable-housing tax credits, investments and commitments; deferred tax assets, liabilities, carryforwards, expirations and valuation allowances; unrecognized tax benefits, possible audit changes, interest and penalties; and the status of tax examinations. It also discloses restricted cash and securities, legal limits on affiliate transactions, holding-company funding relationships, regulatory constraints on distributions, and subsidiary dividend capacity.

nodes.title: Note 26 - Restrictions on cash and intercompany funds transfers
key_items: Restricted cash and other restricted assets
nodes.summary: The note describes regulatory restrictions on the Firm’s cash and assets, including restricted cash of $19.7 billion in 2021 versus $24.4 billion in 2020, amounts segregated for customers and held as central-bank reserves, and other customer-related restricted assets. It explains federal limits on bank lending and covered transactions with the Parent Company and affiliates, the roles and funding relationships of the Parent Company and IHC, regulatory and threshold-based limits on dividends and credit, and approximately $20 billion of aggregate dividends bank subsidiaries could pay without prior approval at January 1, 2022.

nodes.title: Note 27 - Regulatory capital
nodes.summary: Explains Federal Reserve and OCC oversight and Basel III Standardized and Advanced capital calculations, minimum risk-based and leverage requirements, and well-capitalized thresholds for JPMorgan Chase and its insured bank subsidiaries. Tables give 2021 and 2020 requirements, including GSIB surcharge, capital buffers, and exceptions; describe CECL capital transition provisions and PPP loan risk weights; and report both years’ capital amounts, risk-weighted assets, capital ratios, leverage metrics, and SLRs. Both entities met requirements and were well-capitalized. Notes explain adjusted assets and temporary SLR exposure exclusions.

nodes.title: Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase describes its lending-related commitments, guarantees, and other off-balance-sheet instruments, whose contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk but not expected exposure or funding needs because most are not drawn or defaulted on. It maintains an allowance for expected losses on certain commitments (see Note 13) and presents contractual amounts and carrying values for 2021 and 2020. Credit card and home equity figures reflect total available credit, which is not expected to be fully used simultaneously. The Firm may reduce or cancel credit card lines, including for borrowers at least 60 days past due, and may reduce or close HELOCs after significant property-value declines or demonstrable borrower credit deterioration.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
nodes.summary: Presents 2021 and 2020 contractual amounts, remaining-maturity breakdowns, and carrying values for off-balance-sheet lending commitments, guarantees, letters of credit, securities-lending indemnities, derivatives, unsettled securities transactions, loan-sale indemnifications, clearing-house guarantees, and other commitments. Notes explain categories, risk participations, collateral, geographic concentration, and carrying-value measures. Describes credit commitments and U.S. GAAP guarantee recognition, measurement, amortization, and contingent-obligation accounting. Details standby letters of credit and financial guarantees, including investment-grade classification, allowances, liabilities, collateralized commitments, and comparative amounts.

nodes.title: Credit Commitments and Guarantees
key_items: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
nodes.summary: Unfunded credit commitments support working capital, corporate purposes, commercial paper and bond financing, clearing organizations, and multipurpose facilities that may include standby letters of credit. The text explains U.S. GAAP’s definition and fair-value recognition of guarantees, identifies covered off-balance-sheet arrangements, and describes accounting for premiums, amortization, lending-related expected credit losses, and probable, estimable non-lending obligations such as indemnifications. Contractual amounts and carrying values are referenced. Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees conditionally support clients’ performance to third parties across financing and trade arrangements.

nodes.title: Standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and other letters of credit
key_items: Securities lending indemnifications; Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021 and 2020 contractual amounts, carrying values, allowances, guarantee liabilities, and collateralized commitments for standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees, and other letters of credit, with credit ratings based on internal risk ratings. It explains securities-lending indemnifications, including collateral requirements, daily valuation, and default remedies, plus indemnification on invested cash collateral. It describes written put options and stable value contracts treated as derivative guarantees, their purposes, exposure limits, fair-value measurement and risk mitigation, and presents their 2021 and 2020 notional amounts and payables. It also notes the Firm’s credit-protection activity and refers to Note 5.

nodes.title: Unsettled securities financing agreements
nodes.summary: The Firm enters into resale and securities-borrowed agreements, which at settlement involve advancing cash and receiving securities collateral, and repurchase and securities-loaned agreements, which involve receiving cash and providing collateral. These future-settling agreements generally are not derivatives and are not recorded on the consolidated balance sheets until settlement; most have regular-way settlement terms. Further details are in Note 11.

nodes.title: Loan sales- and securitization-related indemnifications
key_items: Mortgage repurchase liability; Private label securitizations
nodes.summary: The Firm may have to repurchase mortgage loans sold to U.S. GSEs or indemnify purchasers if representations and warranties are breached; private-label securitization repurchase demands are assessed separately in litigation reserves (see Note 30). Mortgage servicing may be recourse or nonrecourse: nonrecourse risk mainly involves temporary servicing advances, while recourse shares credit losses with loan owners. Most securitizations are nonrecourse, transferring future credit risk to security purchasers. Recourse loan balances were $827 million in 2021 and $889 million in 2020; related liabilities were $19 million and $23 million, respectively.

nodes.title: Other off-balance sheet arrangements
key_items: Exchange & Clearing House Memberships; Sponsored member repo program
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet arrangements: tax, software-license and business-sale indemnities, whose maximum exposure is hard to estimate but expected to pose remote loss risk; merchant card charge-backs, mitigated by reserves, collateral and valuation allowances, with processed volumes reported for 2019–2021; clearing-member client credit risk, margin practices, closeout rights and remote expected losses; exchange and clearing-house mutual loss obligations; guarantees for sponsored-member repo clients, collateralized to reduce risk; and Parent Company guarantees of subsidiary obligations, including fully guaranteed JPMFC securities, with no separate liability recognized for obligations already recorded or disclosed.

Covers JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet lending commitments, guarantees and other arrangements, explaining maximum contractual exposure, expected losses, credit-line limits and accounting treatment. Reports comparative 2021–2020 amounts, maturities, carrying values, allowances, liabilities, collateral and ratings for commitments, letters of credit, securities-lending indemnities, derivative guarantees and other instruments. Also discusses unsettled securities financing, loan-sale and securitization indemnifications, tax and other indemnities, merchant charge-backs, clearing and exchange risks, sponsored-member repos, and Parent Company guarantees.

nodes.title: Note 29 - Pledged assets and collateral
nodes.summary: The Firm pledges financial assets to support borrowing capacity and secure financing agreements, short sales, derivatives, and deposits; secured parties may sometimes sell or reuse them. At year-end 2021, total pledged assets were $714.7 billion, versus $735.8 billion in 2020, including assets usable by secured parties, assets not usable by them, and assets pledged at Federal Reserve banks and FHLBs. Major categories were investment securities, loans, and trading assets and other. Totals exclude consolidated VIE assets; related notes cover VIEs, securities financing, and long-term debt. The Firm also accepts collateral, generally through financing agreements, customer receivables, and derivatives, and uses it for financing, short sales, derivatives, and deposits. Collateral permitted for use was $1,471.3 billion in 2021 and $1,451.7 billion in 2020; amounts actually sold, repledged, delivered, or otherwise used were $1,111.0 billion and $1,038.9 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Note 30 - Litigation
Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation
nodes.summary: As of December 31, 2021, the Firm faced numerous private lawsuits, class actions, government investigations and regulatory proceedings across businesses and jurisdictions. It estimated reasonably possible losses above reserves at $0–$1.5 billion, while noting some matters could not be estimated; uncertainty reflects early-stage cases, multiple defendants, unresolved issues and unpredictable outcomes, so estimates may change and actual losses may differ. Material matters include India’s Amrapali investigation: an approximately $31.5 million fine is under appeal, about $25 million was attached, and the Firm is cooperating with a money-laundering inquiry following preliminary findings of possible currency-control and money-laundering violations. In Nigeria litigation, the Firm paid out approximately $1.1 billion from an escrow account on client instructions; Nigeria seeks about $875 million, alleging fraud and that the bank should have recognized it. The bank’s summary-judgment bid failed, and trial began in February 2022.

nodes.title: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
nodes.summary: The text reviews JPMorgan’s FX, recordkeeping, interchange-fee, and benchmark-rate legal matters. FX matters include a 2015 antitrust guilty plea, a temporary ERISA exemption requiring renewal, a pending South African inquiry, and U.S. and international civil actions and settlements. In 2021, SEC and CFTC resolutions over unapproved messaging and supervision failures imposed $200 million in penalties; related inquiries continue. Interchange litigation includes amended monetary settlements, pending appeals and injunctive claims, and individual suits. EURIBOR investigations continue, including a pending appeal of the European Commission’s antitrust decision.

nodes.title: Regulatory Inquiries and Antitrust Litigation
nodes.summary: The page describes foreign-exchange matters, including a remaining South African competition inquiry, the need for a further ERISA exemption after January 2023, and U.S. and international FX class and individual litigation, with one $10 million settlement. It covers SEC and CFTC record-preservation findings, supervision failures, $200 million in penalties, and ongoing cooperation. It also summarizes interchange-fee litigation, settlements, pending merchant appeals and injunctive claims, and related individual actions.

nodes.title: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase faces global governmental investigations and litigation concerning LIBOR, EURIBOR, and other benchmark rates. A Swiss EURIBOR investigation continues; the European Commission found an antitrust infringement in 2016, and the Firm’s appeal is pending. In U.S. dollar LIBOR cases, some claims were dismissed or settled, while others continue; a court certified certain antitrust classes, but dismissed an ICE-administered LIBOR class action. Individual plaintiffs’ claims alleging rate-setting and market monopolization remain in litigation; a preliminary-injunction request was denied in 2021. Settlements involving Swiss franc LIBOR and Singapore and Australian benchmarks await court approval.

nodes.title: Metals and U.S. Treasuries Investigations and Litigation and Related Inquiries
nodes.summary: The Firm resolved DOJ, CFTC and SEC investigations into former employees’ 2008–2016 precious metals and U.S. Treasuries trading practices, agreeing to a DOJ deferred prosecution agreement involving two wire-fraud counts, compliance obligations and dismissal after three years if obligations are met. The agencies’ resolutions totaled about $920 million, partly for victim compensation. Related U.S. precious-metals and Treasury manipulation class actions were consolidated, with settlements preliminarily approved in December 2021; similar precious-metals proceedings were proposed in Canada. Shareholders also sued over alleged misleading SEC disclosures and futures orders; the cases were consolidated, and defendants moved to dismiss.

nodes.title: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
nodes.summary: The text describes a securities-lending antitrust class action against JPMorgan entities alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading. The court denied defendants’ motion to dismiss; plaintiffs seek class certification, which defendants oppose. JPMorgan also faces many other proceedings, plans to defend them, and may face future cases. It maintains reserves, accrues probable and estimable losses under U.S. GAAP, reviews reserves quarterly, and reported legal expenses of $426 million in 2021, $1.1 billion in 2020, and $239 million in 2019. Outcomes, timing, and losses are uncertain; although the Firm believes other pending cases will not materially harm consolidated financial condition, losses could exceed reserves, have reputational effects, or materially affect results in a given period.

The section reviews JPMorgan Chase’s litigation, investigations and regulatory proceedings across jurisdictions, including Nigeria and India matters, foreign-exchange conduct and recordkeeping, interchange fees, LIBOR/EURIBOR and other benchmarks, precious metals and U.S. Treasuries, and securities lending. It describes allegations, enforcement actions, penalties, settlements, appeals, ongoing inquiries and lawsuits, and the Firm’s defenses and cooperation. It also discusses loss estimates and uncertainty, reserves and legal expenses, and the possibility of losses exceeding reserves or affecting reputation or results.

nodes.title: Note 31 - International operations
nodes.summary: Note 31 reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2019–2021 revenue, expense, pretax income, net income and total assets across Europe/Middle East/Africa, Asia-Pacific, Latin America/Caribbean, total international, and North America, with annual totals. International activity is defined by clients and relationship, booking, or trading locations; figures rely on estimates to allocate revenue and expenses consistent with segment reporting. Long-lived assets are not significant relative to total assets and are mostly in the U.S. North America substantially reflects the U.S.; prior-year figures were revised for presentation consistency. Revenue includes net interest and noninterest revenue; expense includes noninterest expense and credit-loss provision. U.K. assets are also disclosed for each year.

nodes.title: Note 32 - Business segments
JPMorgan Chase Business Segments
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase manages its businesses by line of business, reporting four major segments and a Corporate segment; segment definitions reflect products, customers and management reporting, with results presented on a managed basis. Consumer & Community Banking serves consumers and businesses through deposits, lending, payments, mortgages, cards and auto loans. Corporate & Investment Bank provides investment banking, payments, markets, risk management, prime brokerage, research and securities services to global clients. Commercial Banking provides lending, payments, investment banking and asset management for middle-market, corporate and commercial real estate clients. Asset & Wealth Management, with $4.3 trillion in client assets, serves institutional, retail and high-net-worth clients through investment management, private banking and related services; most assets are actively managed. Corporate comprises Treasury and CIO, which manages liquidity, funding, capital and structural market risks, plus centrally managed corporate functions and expenses.

nodes.title: Corporate
nodes.summary: The note describes JPMorgan Chase’s four reportable business segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus Corporate, explaining how segments are organized, their customers, products, and services. It outlines managed-basis reporting, which adjusts revenue to a fully taxable-equivalent basis without changing net income, and capital allocation based on peer and regulatory requirements, risk measures, and return targets. A table presents 2019–2021 segment results and reconciliations, including revenues, credit-loss provisions, expenses, income, equity, assets, return on equity, and overhead ratios.

nodes.title: Segment results
nodes.summary: The notes describe segment results for 2021, 2020, and 2019 on a managed basis, which adjusts U.S. GAAP results to present revenue on a fully taxable-equivalent basis, making taxable and tax-exempt revenue comparable; related tax effects appear in income tax expense, without changing reported net income. Capital is allocated to segments considering peer capital levels and regulatory requirements, with ROE and expected-return targets used to assess performance. The methodology includes Basel III standardized and advanced risk-weighted assets, the GSIB surcharge, and severe-stress capital simulations; assumptions are periodically reassessed, so allocations may change.

nodes.title: Segment results and reconciliation (a)
nodes.summary: A continued segment-results table for JPMorgan Chase’s Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management segments reports 2021, 2020, and 2019 financial results. Measures include noninterest revenue, net interest income, total net revenue, credit-loss provisions, noninterest expense, pretax income or loss, taxes, net income or loss, average equity, total assets, return on equity, and overhead ratio; some figures are marked as revised or footnoted.

nodes.title: (Table continued from previous page)

It then presents JPMorgan Chase Parent Company-only income and comprehensive income statements, balance sheets, and cash-flow statements for 2019–2021, including subsidiary income, assets, liabilities, equity, financing, dividends, and cash and tax payments. Footnotes explain affiliate treatment, debt maturities, guarantees, tax reimbursements, and a merger-related capital distribution.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s four business segments and Corporate, including their customers, products, services, and management roles. Explains managed-basis reporting and revenue’s fully taxable-equivalent adjustment, capital allocation and performance measures, and the risk and regulatory assumptions used. Presents 2019–2021 segment results and reconciliations, including revenues, provisions, expenses, income, equity, assets, ROE, and overhead ratios, with revisions and footnotes. Also provides Parent Company-only income, comprehensive income, balance-sheet, and cash-flow statements, with notes on affiliates, debt, guarantees, taxes, dividends, and a merger-related capital distribution.

nodes.title: Note 33 - Parent company
nodes.summary: Note 33 presents JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Parent Company-only income and comprehensive income statements for 2019–2021, balance sheets for 2020–2021, and cash flow statements for 2019–2021, with figures in millions. The statements cover subsidiary dividends and income, expenses, taxes, equity in subsidiary earnings, assets, liabilities, equity, operating, investing and financing cash flows, and cash balances. Footnotes explain affiliate trusts, long-term debt maturities, subsidiary guarantees, cash taxes and reimbursements, and a $13.5 billion return-of-capital distribution following a bank merger.

The notes explain JPMorgan Chase’s accounting basis, policies, estimates, consolidation, fair-value measurement and option, credit concentrations, derivatives, and revenue and interest. They detail employee benefits and compensation; investment securities, financing, loans, credit-loss allowances, VIEs, goodwill, MSRs, premises, deposits, leases, liabilities, debt, stock, EPS, AOCI, and taxes. They also cover regulatory restrictions and capital, commitments and guarantees, collateral, litigation, international operations, business segments, and Parent Company-only financial statements, with comparative disclosures, methodologies, risks, and related accounting treatments.

Includes consolidated statements of income, comprehensive income, equity, cash flows, and balance sheets, with comparative periods and CECL adoption. Consolidated average balance sheets, interest and rates
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s unaudited consolidated average balance sheets, interest income/expense, and rates for 2019–2021 on a taxable-equivalent basis, covering asset, liability, and equity categories and net interest spread, income, and yield. Explains the 24% tax-equivalent adjustment and notes on nonaccrual loans, tax-exempt securities, included customer balances and fees, presentation revisions, trading liabilities, equity ratios and returns, hedging effects, negative yields, and securities’ amortized-cost rates.

nodes.title: Interest rates and interest differential analysis of net interest income – U.S. and non-U.S.
nodes.summary: Unaudited taxable-equivalent tables compare JPMorgan Chase’s U.S. and non-U.S. average balances, interest income or expense, and rates for 2019–2021. They cover interest-earning asset and interest-bearing liability categories, noninterest-bearing funding, total investable funds, net interest income and yield, and non-U.S. shares of assets and liabilities. Geographic attribution follows the office recording each transaction; intercompany funding is generally centrally managed dollar deposits. Notes explain negative securities-borrowed income and prime-brokerage expense, commercial paper inclusion, and noninterest-bearing funding. A reference directs readers to the net interest income discussion elsewhere in the 10-K.

nodes.title: Changes in net interest income, volume and rate analysis
nodes.summary: The unaudited table attributes changes in taxable-equivalent net interest income to volume and rate for 2021 versus 2020 and 2020 versus 2019, across U.S. and non-U.S. interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities, showing volume, rate, and net changes in interest income, expense, and net interest income. It explains that calculations use annual average balances and rates; inseparable effects are assigned to volume, rates reflect market and product-composition changes, and category-by-category results exclude relationships between categories, making attribution judgmental and sensitive to groupings. Footnotes explain negative income/yields on client-driven securities borrowed balances, related prime-brokerage customer-payable expense classification, and inclusion of commercial paper.

Compares U.S. and non-U.S. balances, interest, rates, funding, and geographic attribution, and analyzes changes in net interest income by volume and rate for 2021 versus 2020 and 2020 versus 2019, including methodological caveats and category-specific footnotes.

nodes.title: Glossary of Terms and Acronyms

nodes.summary: A glossary from JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K defines financial, banking, regulatory, risk, technology, and business terms and acronyms. nodes.title: Expense categories:

Provides a glossary of financial, regulatory, risk, lending, and corporate acronyms and terms, including agencies and entities; credit, liquidity, capital, and derivative concepts; LTV definitions and calculation caveats; managed-basis reporting, master netting agreements, and the measurement alternative; and Merchant Services offerings.

nodes.title: Glossary and Loan-to-Value Definitions
nodes.summary: Defines financial, regulatory, and organizational terms and acronyms, including G7, mortgage and banking terms, JPMorgan entities, and risk measures. Defines LTV as loan principal relative to collateral value, and distinguishes origination-date LTV, based on actual appraisals, from current estimated LTV, based on MSA-level home-price indices using actual or forecast data; the latter is imprecise and should be treated as an estimate.

nodes.title: Combined LTV ratio
nodes.summary: Defines combined LTV as a property’s loan-to-value ratio across all liens and unused lines, used for junior-lien home equity products. Explains managed-basis non-GAAP results, including fully taxable-equivalent reclassifications and their use to assess segment performance and compare competitors. Defines a master netting agreement as allowing covered transactions to be settled by one payment after default. Expands MBS, MD&A, MEV, MMLF, and Moody’s; describes the measurement alternative for certain equity securities and Merchant Services’ payment processing, fraud and risk management, analytics, and multicurrency capabilities.

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF LISTED PREFERRED STOCK
Authorized Shares
nodes.summary: The text notes that the summary is incomplete and directs readers to the charter and series-specific certificates of designations incorporated into the Form 10-K. The board may issue up to 200 million preferred shares and set their terms, with authorized amounts amendable under the charter and Delaware law. Eighteen preferred series are outstanding; six listed, fully paid and nonassessable series are registered through depositary shares, each representing 1/400 of a share. Listed stock ranks equally with parity preferred, senior to common and junior preferred, but below debt. Dividends are board-declared, noncumulative, and payable on specified record dates; missed dividends are forfeited. Dividend priority and pro rata allocation apply among parity series, and restrictions apply to distributions on junior stock unless listed dividends are fully paid or provided for.

nodes.title: Outstanding Preferred Stock and Ranking
nodes.summary: The company may amend its charter to adjust authorized preferred shares as permitted by the charter and Delaware law. At the Form 10-K filing date, 18 preferred-stock series were outstanding, represented by depositary shares. Six registered series—DD, EE, GG, JJ, LL, and MM—with stated non-cumulative dividend rates have depositary shares representing 1/400th of a preferred share each; collectively, they are the Listed Preferred Stock, which is fully paid and nonassessable. Their depositary-share terms are described elsewhere. They rank equally with parity-ranking preferred stock, ahead of common and junior preferred stock for dividends and liquidation distributions, but behind existing and future indebtedness.

nodes.title: Dividend Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock dividends are payable in cash only when declared, to record holders, and are noncumulative, so undeclared dividends are forfeited. Dividend priorities require full payment or setting aside for the latest period before dividends on equal- or junior-ranking stock; shortfalls among parity series are allocated pro rata. Until preferred dividends are covered, junior-stock dividends and certain stock repurchases are restricted, subject to listed exceptions, while ordinary-course market transactions remain permitted. The text defines junior, parity, and senior ranking, states that preferred holders do not share in permitted junior or parity dividends, and specifies dividend calculation and rounding methods.

nodes.title: Rights Upon Liquidation
nodes.summary: Upon liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, each Listed Preferred Stock series receives $10,000 per share plus declared, unpaid dividends before junior shares; undeclared dividends do not accumulate, and holders have no claim to remaining assets. If funds are insufficient, equal-ranking shares share distributions ratably. Asset sales and mergers or consolidations are not treated as liquidation events. As a holding company, the company’s subsidiary assets may first be subject to subsidiary creditors’ claims. Preferred holders rank below company debt and other non-equity claims and may also be subordinated to U.S. government interests in insolvency proceedings.

nodes.title: Redemption
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase may redeem each preferred-stock series on specified dates/prices, or redeem an entire series at $10,000 per share ($25 per depositary share) plus declared unpaid dividends after a capital treatment event—when specified post-issuance legal or official changes create more than an insubstantial risk that the shares will no longer qualify as additional Tier 1 capital. Redemptions require regulatory approval. Holders receive 30–60 days’ mailed notice (or DTC-approved notice), stating redemption details; holders cannot demand redemption. Partial redemptions are selected pro rata or by lot. Dividends and other rights end on redemption, except payment rights. If full dividends are unpaid, partial redemption and acquisitions are barred, except equal-terms offers to all holders.

nodes.title: Voting Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock generally has no voting rights except as required by law or specified; when voting, each share has one vote, based on shares outstanding. After six unpaid quarterly dividends, holders of the affected series and voting-parity stock may elect two directors until four consecutive quarters of dividends are paid; rules govern director removal, vacancies, and termination or revival of these rights. A two-thirds vote is required to authorize senior securities or make materially adverse charter changes, subject to specified exceptions and series-specific approval rules. Redemption with funds placed irrevocably in trust suspends these votes, and additional shares may be issued without holder consent. Delaware law provides separate-class votes for certain charter changes, subject to the company’s majority-vote provision. Federal Reserve rules may regulate significant holders or require acquisition approvals or notices when arrears confer director-election rights.

nodes.title: Alerian ETN Structure, Index, and Denominations
nodes.summary: The Alerian ETNs are unsecured, unsubordinated Series E debt obligations of JPMorgan Chase & Co., subject to its credit risk, with no guaranteed principal repayment; they are neither bank deposits nor government-insured. “Holders” refers to registered owners, and undefined capitalized terms are explained elsewhere. Returns track the Alerian MLP Index, which measures energy-oriented MLP performance and is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices with its sponsor using float-adjusted market capitalization. Notes are denominated in U.S. dollars, with a minimum denomination of $19.03661 per note.

nodes.title: Coupon Payments and the Accrued Tracking Fee
nodes.summary: Quarterly coupon payments per ETN equal the Reference Distribution Amount minus the Accrued Tracking Fee, which accrues daily at 0.85% annually on Daily Note Value, reflecting cumulative index performance since April 1, 2009. Daily Note Value and interim coupon amounts are published under specified Bloomberg tickers; index VWAP is based on component weighted average prices calculated from their primary exchanges. If distributions do not cover fees, no coupon is paid and the shortfall carries forward, alongside further accrual, until covered. Coupons are paid in arrears on the fifteenth Index Business Day after valuation; the final coupon is included in the maturity cash settlement. Interim amounts are calculated and published each Index Business Day, but actual coupons are determined quarterly.

nodes.title: Payment Upon Early Repurchase
nodes.summary: Holders may request weekly early repurchase of at least 50,000 Alerian ETNs, subject to market-disruption provisions and strict notice, confirmation, and DTC delivery procedures. Payment per note is the Repurchase Amount, which is unknown when requested and reflects index performance over a five-business-day measurement period, tracking and repurchase fees, and specified coupon and component-distribution adjustments; payment is zero if the amount is nonpositive. The repurchase fee is 0.125% of adjusted principal and varies with index performance, fees, and distributions. Early repurchase may cause loss of some or all principal. Notices and confirmations have Thursday-related deadlines, must be acknowledged, and are irrevocable; late or invalid submissions are ineffective. Brokers may impose earlier deadlines, and the Note Calculation Agent decides questions of validity and delivery.

nodes.title: Payment at Maturity
nodes.summary: At maturity, unless repurchased earlier, each Alerian ETN pays its Cash Settlement Amount, floored at zero. This amount adjusts principal for the Index return from the Initial to Final VWAP Level, any final coupon and qualifying Index Component cash distributions, and the deduction of the Accrued Tracking Fee. The Final VWAP Level averages VWAPs over five Index Business Days near maturity; the Initial VWAP Level averages them over the three Index Business Days ending on the Inception Date. The VWAP Calculation Agent determines both. Holders may lose some or all of their investment, particularly if Index performance fails to offset the tracking fee.

nodes.title: VWAP Calculation Agent
nodes.summary: The JPMorgan Global Index Research Group, an affiliate, serves as VWAP Calculation Agent on days that are not Disrupted Days. During the Alerian ETNs’ term, it determines the VWAP of any Index Component, the VWAP Level, and the Final VWAP Level on applicable Index Business Days.

nodes.title: Market Disruption Events
nodes.summary: Defines how disruption affects Index Component VWAP and share weighting: calculations move to the first succeeding non-disrupted Index Business Day, with deferred values applied to both the original disrupted date and that scheduled averaging date. Final averaging cannot be delayed beyond three Index Business Days; if that day is not a valid business day, the calculation agent uses a good-faith estimate. Defines Averaging Date, Disrupted Day, and Market Disruption Event, covering exchange closures, trading suspensions or limits, impaired market access, early closes, and material interference with hedging, all subject to agent determinations. Announced trading-hours changes are excluded; specified volatility-based trading limits count as disruptions. Defines Scheduled Closing Time as the regular-session scheduled weekday close, excluding after-hours trading.

nodes.title: Covenant Breaches and Indenture Modifications
nodes.summary: Holders’ rights to receive due payments and sue to enforce payment cannot be impaired without their consent; the issuer must annually report to the Trustee whether it knows of a default. A Covenant Breach occurs when a nonpayment covenant breach continues 90 days after required written notice, but cannot trigger acceleration; the Trustee may pursue judicial remedies for continuing breaches or defaults. Indenture changes generally require approval by a majority of each affected series, while specified changes to key payment, maturity, currency, conversion, suit, repurchase, or consent rights require every affected holder’s consent. Certain administrative or non-adverse amendments may be made without holder consent.

Written or electronic notice—including a good-faith attempt to the last recorded address—preserves recovery rights; tax amounts that cannot be reclaimed are excluded, and repayment may be in cash or shares, not as a penalty. The Firm may seek injunctions, with other remedies preserved. Administrative provisions cover tax withholding methods, set-off against amounts owed subject to account protections, PSUs’ lack of ownership or voting rights before issuance, possible cancellation during vesting suspension, brokerage/book-entry delivery, and temporary share restrictions that do not affect voting or dividends but may trigger recovery. The agreement binds successors, creates no employment or future-award entitlement, and is not severance compensation. Section 409A compliance is intended; the text begins a specified-employee separation-from-service provision but ends before its terms are complete.

nodes.title: Award Enforcement and Administrative Terms
nodes.summary: The text addresses repayment and tax-payment limits, confirms repayment is not a penalty and preserves other clawback obligations, and grants the Firm injunctive relief for violations. It covers tax withholding methods, setoff rights and limits, and PSU ownership, share issuance, account creation, cancellation, and possible stock restrictions or recovery. The award binds JPMorgan Chase successors but creates no employment guarantee, future-award entitlement, or severance compensation.

nodes.title: Section 409A Compliance
nodes.summary: The terms address Section 409A compliance, including a six-month distribution delay for specified employees and payment timing for vested awards; equitable share adjustments for corporate events and other changes (excluding the Qualitative Performance Factor); and the Committee’s broad, nonuniform authority to interpret and administer the award. They cover amendment limits and written-form requirements, reformation of unenforceable provisions, and possible accelerated distribution or holding-period waiver for government ethics or divestiture requirements, subject to Section 409A and continuing award obligations. Acceptance also permits personal-data processing and disclosure to third parties.

nodes.title: Award Agreement Administration and Adjustments
nodes.summary: The page sets Section 409A timing rules for share distributions after separation or vesting; provides for equitable share adjustments after corporate events and other award adjustments for changed circumstances, except for the Qualitative Performance Factor; gives the Committee broad, potentially non-uniform authority to interpret and administer the award; describes amendment powers, limits, and written-signature requirements; and allows unenforceable provisions to be reformed.

nodes.title: Accelerated Distribution for Ethics or Conflict Reasons Resulting From Employment by a Government Entity
nodes.summary: The text permits accelerated PSU distribution or waiver of holding restrictions when government ethics or conflict rules require divestiture, subject to Section 409A, specified termination provisions, and continued recovery and employment obligations. It explains personal-data processing, transfers, and cancellation rights; New York governing law; arbitration or exclusive federal-court venue; jury-trial and class-action waivers; the Firm’s attorney-fee recovery rights; and award non-transferability, with death-related exceptions. Definitions cover tangible common equity, payout percentage, calculated PSUs, calculation agent, cause, and financial services companies.

nodes.title: Award Legal Terms and Restrictions
nodes.summary: The text permits personal-data sharing and transfers abroad, with limited rights to revoke authorization; revocation cancels the award except for required reporting and legal obligations. New York law governs. Disputes may be arbitrated at the Firm’s election or heard exclusively in the Southern District of New York. Employment-related claims waive jury trials and class or representative actions. The Firm may recover reasonable legal fees when it prevails enforcing award agreements, and the recipient waives fee advancement and indemnification. Awards cannot generally be transferred or encumbered, but may pass at death by will, inheritance, or beneficiary designation.

nodes.title: Definitions
nodes.summary: Defines award and performance terms, including tangible common equity, payout calculations and caps, calculation agent, cause, financial-services competitors, ROTCE, financial thresholds, government office, business lines, nonprofits, peer companies, performance periods/rankings/table and tie handling, recognized service, and target PSUs. It then sets government-service continued-vesting rules: eligibility and notice/documentation requirements, service-based vesting percentages, conditions for public office or candidacy, continued award restrictions, and cancellation or repayment if conditions are not met.

nodes.title: Government Office Vesting Eligibility
nodes.summary: Employees may continue vesting in all or part of an award after voluntarily resigning to accept or seek elective Government Office. These requirements do not apply to those meeting Full Career Eligibility when employment ends. Continued vesting requires at least 60 days’ advance written notice, during which the employee cooperates with the Firm and works for no other employer; the Firm may shorten the period. The employee must also provide satisfactory confirmation of legal compliance and documentation that the resignation is for the stated Government Office purpose.

The section explains malus, clawback, cancellation, and recovery rights, including triggers, deadlines, remedies, and administrative handling of PSUs. It sets post-termination continued-vesting rules for job elimination, full-career retirement, government office, and disability, with notice, service, documentation, release, and certification requirements. It covers death benefits; conduct, confidentiality, solicitation, cooperation, and notice obligations; tax, withholding, set-off, issuance, and share restrictions; Section 409A timing, adjustments, and administration; ethics-related accelerated distribution; data processing; governing law, dispute resolution, waivers, fees, and transfer limits; and award definitions and government-service vesting conditions.

nodes.title: Portion of Your Award Subject to Continued Vesting:
nodes.summary: The award portion continuing to vest on its original schedule depends on continuous service immediately before termination: 50% for 3 to under 4 years, 75% for 4 to under 5 years, and 100% for 5 or more years. This portion is the “CV Award”; the remainder is cancelled when employment terminates.

nodes.title: Conditions for Continued Vesting of Award:
nodes.summary: Continued vesting of a CV Award requires at least two years in a non-elective Government Office after leaving the Firm, unless the award vests during a shorter period of government service; alternatively, candidates for elective office must appear on the primary or final public ballot. Existing performance and protection-based vesting terms continue to apply. When conditions are met, outstanding awards—including shares accelerated for ethics or conflict reasons—remain subject to the Award Agreement’s terms and vesting-period employment restrictions, as for someone meeting Full Career Eligibility. If conditions are not met, outstanding PSUs are cancelled, and the recipient must repay the pre-withholding fair market value, measured on distribution date, of accelerated shares that otherwise would have remained outstanding.

The terms govern a nontransferable 2022 PSU award, including acceptance, plan priority, vesting eligibility, performance calculations and qualitative assessments, share delivery and holding restrictions, capital-based reductions, and CEO cancellation and committee approval. They address bonus recoupment and EMEA malus, clawback, and recovery rights; post-termination vesting and death benefits; conduct and service conditions; taxes, withholding, administration, data, legal and dispute provisions; and government-service vesting requirements, including CV Award percentages, eligibility conditions, cancellation, and repayment.

title: Exhibit 10.23

nodes.title: Performance-Based Incentive Compensation Plan Preamble
nodes.summary: Exhibit 10.23 presents JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s amended Performance-Based Incentive Compensation Plan, effective January 1, 2021. Its preamble describes the plan’s goals: align annual awards with company, business-unit, and employee performance; attract, motivate, and retain employees; promote accountability and long-term shareholder value, safety, and soundness through potential award cancellation or clawback. The plan does not change at-will employment, reflects participating companies’ prior policies, and is intended to comply with Internal Revenue Code Section 409A and related regulations, including Section 4.3’s subjective-performance criteria rules.

nodes.title: SECTION 2 DEFINITIONS
nodes.summary: Defines key Plan terms, including Awards and agreements, eligible employees, participating entities, performance years, stock awards, subsidiaries, and the 162(m) Plan. JPMorgan Chase administers the Plan, with authority over budgets, participant selection, performance criteria, award terms, interpretation, rules, corrections, and other decisions; it may delegate authority, and decisions are binding. Annual incentives are discretionary and based on holistic Company and business-unit performance, including financial and client results, risk and conduct, strategic progress, and operating principles.

nodes.title: Plan Definitions and Administration
nodes.summary: Defines the Plan, Stock-Based Awards, Subsidiary, and 162(m) Plan. Section 3 assigns JPMorgan Chase authority to set performance-year budgets, select eligible employees, establish and assess performance criteria, determine award terms and amounts, interpret and amend plan rules, and make necessary administrative decisions. It may correct inconsistencies, delegate its authority, and make decisions that are final and binding. Section 4 appears as a heading only.

nodes.title: PERFORMANCE-BASED COMPENSATION ORGANIZATIONAL AND INDIVIDUAL CRITERIA; PARTICIPATION
nodes.summary: The plan makes annual incentive compensation discretionary, based on a holistic review of company and business-unit results, risk and conduct, strategic progress, operating principles, market trends, staffing decisions, and other qualitative factors. JPMorgan Chase may designate eligible employees, but awards depend on organizational and individual performance; amounts and forms are solely discretionary, and awards are not guaranteed except as specified in certain new-hire or retention agreements. Individual assessment may consider profitability, growth investment, major projects, talent management, integrity and risk, revenue, work quality, work ethic, and reviews. Inapplicable criteria are disregarded; JPMorgan Chase or its delegate determines criteria and results at year-end, with additional subjective criteria set within 90 days of the performance year’s start. Employees and their family members cannot determine whether subjective criteria are met.

nodes.title: SECTION 5 AWARDS
nodes.summary: Awards are determined after each performance year based on employee contribution and performance, with payment generally in the following calendar year and usually requiring active employment on the payment date; no award interest exists until payment. Awards specify cash, stock-based or other forms, may allow certain overseas property/trust delivery or agreed cash deferral, and stock awards follow an approved plan. Awards promote continued service, must be documented in signed agreements, and cannot be promised orally. Participating Companies may withhold taxes and offset debts. Awards are generally nontransferable and create no right to an award, continued employment, or future awards; JPMorgan Chase retains discretion to amend or terminate the Plan, subject to a timing limit for individual performance criteria. The Plan is unfunded, confers only unsecured-creditor status before payment, excludes awards from benefit compensation unless permitted, and its documents supersede other representations. Failure or delay to enforce rights is not a waiver.

nodes.title: Plan Award Rules and Status
key_items: NO RIGHT TO EMPLOYMENT CONTINUED PLAN PARTICIPATION
nodes.summary: Covers tax withholding and offsets for amounts owed to participating companies; restrictions on transferring awards; no guarantee of awards, continued employment, future participation, or similar awards, with awards at JPMorgan Chase’s discretion and employment terminable subject to stated exceptions; JPMorgan Chase’s authority to amend or terminate the Plan, with a timing restriction for amending Section 4.3 performance criteria; and the Plan’s unfunded status, recipients’ unsecured-creditor rights, exclusion of awards from benefit calculations unless permitted, and controlling award documents.

nodes.title: WAIVER
nodes.summary: The Plan states that delay or failure to exercise a right does not waive it, and partial exercise does not prevent further exercise. Section 12 preserves remaining provisions if one is invalid and substitutes a valid term that best reflects the Plan’s intent. Section 13 binds merger or consolidation successors and requires successors to substantially all company equity or assets to assume the Plan. Section 14 applies New York law, excluding conflicts principles. Section 15 makes the Plan effective as of its Effective Date until JPMorgan Chase terminates it.

nodes.title: Plan Legal Provisions
nodes.summary: The plan preserves remaining provisions if a term is invalid or unenforceable, replacing it in the affected jurisdiction with a valid term closest to the original intent. In a merger, consolidation, or qualifying succession, the surviving or successor entity must assume and perform the plan, and references to JPMorgan Chase shift to that successor. New York law, excluding conflict-of-laws principles, governs the awards, plan, and related rules and regulations.

nodes.title: SECTION 15 EFFECTIVE DATE
nodes.summary:
SECTION 15 EFFECTIVE DATE
The Plan shall be effective as of the Effective Date and shall continue until terminated by the JPMorgan
Chase.

It defines plan terms and grants JPMorgan Chase broad administrative authority over budgets, eligibility, criteria, awards, and interpretation. Awards reflect organizational and individual results, including financial, client, strategic, risk, conduct, and qualitative factors; they are generally paid the following year, subject to employment, documentation, tax, transfer, and other restrictions, and are not guaranteed.
